maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: Consideration of the motion of Mr. Kelly for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, resumed from Tuesday, March 4.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Like other members who have
preceded me, I beg to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address on the admirable manner in which they portrayed the situation to the House. Both hon. gentlemen discharged the task with honour not only to themselves but also to the House to which they belong. I desire also to extend congratulations, if he is willing to accept my congratulations, to the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) on the way in which he, too, placed his case before the House on Tuesday last. While I am free to admit that I cannot entirely agree with all that the hon. member may have said, nevertheless he brought forward his policies and the policies of his party in a straightforw;frd and manly way, in a way, indeed, that every member of the House could well understand.
I have heard it stated on another occasion that this debate was a more or less innocuous proceeding. I cannot view the debate in such a light. On the contrary, I believe it is. a very important proceeding, enabling the government to hear the views, through hon. gentlemen, that are held in the constituencies they represent. I think it is the duty of every hon. member so to enable the government, by such expressions of opinion, to formulate policies for the good of the Dominion as a whole. You are aware, Mr. Speaker, that I represent in this House the division of St. Lawrence-St. George of Montreal. I do not think it is improper to say that that division is an important one, perhaps one of the most important in this Dominion. It is important by reason of its commercial and financial activity, by reason of the wealth and learning of its people, and by reason of its undoubted 
devotion to the public good. I think I can safely say that no one can accuse the people of that division of narrowness nor of any lack of public spirit; and least of all can anyone accuse them of any failure to contribute to the taxes of this Dominion, for the administration of its affairs and for its development, a very considerable amount. Other qualifications these people have also; and I would ask hon. members to bear with me for a moment in that regard. The people whom I represent in this House are strong in their traditions. They reverence those old British and French traditions which in their opinion go so far as to make a nation idealistic rather than materialistic. And materialism, I think it is not improper for me to say may be found in many parts of this continent, more particularly outside of this Dominion. In addition to that, the people whom I represent are anxious to see maintained as their right and heritage the exercise of the English and French languages; and they desire to enjoy for all times the free and undisputed exercise of their various religions. All these things they regard as essential to good Canadianism. These traditions they cherish and desire to have maintained. While I am free to admit that what I have stated in this regard may strike some as being mere words, nevertheless, to the people I represent, and as well, if I may presume to say so, to the great mass of-the people of Montreal and of the province of Quebec, these same sentiments form a part of their daily lives, and they should be cherished and preserved for all time. It appears to me that they can be preserved only so long as this Dominion remains a free nation, both politically and commercially, under the British Crown. And it can remain free and retain its identity as such only so long as it progresses, and expands, and retains its population. If it loses its population, if it fails to go forward, if it retrogresses, then its identity will undoubtedly be lost; and when that is gone, beyond the shadow of a doubt those' traditions to which I have alluded will also be lost. That is one of the reasons, Sir, why I lay so much stress on the points which I have dealt with so far.
That being the case, there is a certain amount of alarm felt, and I think rightly felt, when we notice the lack of increase in population, and more so when we consider the great exodus of our people in the last few years. Happily the tide inwards is now increasing. But unfortunately the tide outwards is still very serious. Indeed if we look back and realize that for four long years this country poured out its blood and treasure,

The Address-Mr. Marler
and for five years more has been subject to the most heavy imposts-when we realize all that and see our population still leaving us, some of us wonder if all those sacrifices have been made in vain.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that we should be amazed at the emigration of our people which has taken place to the United States, and which has been in progress for some years past. My right hon. friend who leads the opposition (Mr. Meighen) dealt with this very point in his address before the House a few days ago. He spoke with the most meticulous care of this loss of population within the last year, he quoted figures month by month, and it seemed to me that he endeavoured to lead the House to believe that this emigration had taken place only in the past two years.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I gave the figures for three distinct and complete years.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Well, I have no doubt whatever that my right hon. friend stressed only the last couple of years.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They are the worst.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How much the worst?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: About four times.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: From when?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: From 1923. They are about four times worse than 1921.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about 1920 and 1921?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I say 1923 was about four times 1921.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Very well, we shall now have the correct figures so we can see definitely the actual position. Although I am quite free to admit that this is a serious matter, it is no more serious under this government than it was under the past government. The figures I am about to quote are taken from precisely the same source as that from which my right hon. friend derived his figures, the Department of Labour of the United States. For the two years ending 30th June, 1919, 90,234 people left Canada for the United States; the two following years ending 30th June 1921, 162,342 left. Does my right hon. friend shake his head and say that is not correct?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I do not think the figures are quite correct.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would strongly recommend my right hon. friend to look up these figures himself. He will find that they are
correct, because I took them from exactly the same book as he himself used.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Go ahead, what is the deduction?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The deduction is this. For the two years to the 30th June, 1923, 163.000 people left as against 162,000 in the preceding two year period.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, but what about from June on to the end of the year?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The end of what year?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The end of 1923. Why does the hon. gentleman stop in the middle of 1923 when the worst months are those that follow?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My right hon. friend is
always most careful to fit in his figures to some broken period; he never takes a complete year.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No, I took the whole
year, but you are breaking it in the middle.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My right hon. friend is
quite wrong. I am not breaking the year in the middle, I am taking the official year of the United States authorities.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Take the calendar year.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Calendar year? We heard about calendar years in Montreal, and I shall go into that later on. Let us take completed figures, and not partial, such as my right hon. friend did.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
say that my figures are wrong to the extent of one man?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I say these figures are absolutely right. The comparison shows absolutely that the departure of our population to the United States was just as great under his government as it is under the present administration.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is nonsense.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why is it nonsense?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Because the hon. member leaves out the worst months that apply to this government.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not leave out any
months at all, I take the United States fiscal year and I stand by these figures absolutely. I challenge my right hon. friend to say they are wrong.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
But that does not bring the figures up to date.

The Address-Mr. Marler

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No, but distorting figures
in this way-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Try not to, then.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
However, Mr. Speaker,
while this is a very pleasant digression, it does not cover the point that I desire to stress. This exodus to the United States is a very serious matter for us in Canada, and while some in this House and some outside will say that it is only temporary, as a matter of fact it has continued for the last ten years, and the balance in favour of the United States in that period exceeds the total arrivals to the Dominion from that country. Others will say that these Canadians will return to the Dominion. Well, if that be so, why do we find in the United States to-day over
1,200,000	Canadian-bom of whom 307,000 are French^Canadians? And why do we find in the mills of Massachusetts alone 260,000 Canadian-born of whom 108,000 are French-Canadians? Unfortunately these figures are only too true, you may read them to the left or to the right and then up and down and you will be forced to one conclusion only and that is that we are losing some of the best of our population to the nation to the south. Of course, if this had happened before the war possibly we would not have felt the same degree of anxiety as we feel to-day, but our position now is quite different from what it was then. Before the war we had not the heavy debt entailing the payment of some $140,000,000 a year in interest alone; we had not 22,000 miles of railway which can only be operated at a profit with ample traffic; we had not so far extended our systems of canals and elevators-and I am not criticizing this condition of affairs, I am simply taking the facts;-but we have all these things to-day and, wisely or unwisely, as the case may be, we have extended ourselves to accommodate a population five times as great as we can now boast. And yet, with only nine million people, we are still losing population.
It is usual to say that we desire more people to come to this country for the purpose of helping us pay our debts and to share the load which we are carrying. That is not our attitude at all. What we mean is that we desire more population to share with us in bringing to the greatest degree of productivity those great advantages which we enjoy and which, in my opinion, no other country in the world is so richly endowed with. That is the attitude we take

in asking people to come here; that is the attitude we take in asking our own people to remain in this country. But unfortunately, although these reasons should appeal to any Canadian who loves his country and who wishes to see it advance, they do not appeal to as many as we should like. Why is it that we cannot retain our population? I do not think we have to go very far for an answer: as I see it, it is because we do not provide in this country enough steady and profitable work to go round.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not see why the applause should all come from the opposition side. Well, we cannot ask as many as we would like to come to our cities; because we feel that there is not enough profitable and steady work to keep our artisans and others in continuous employment. We even feel that possibly we cannot ask as many to go on our farms as we would like to see go on them, because we are told-and I have no doubt that it is correct-that farming unfortunately does not always pay. In short we have not developed this country industrially and commercially to the extent that we should. The result is that our cities have not enough purchasing power for the farmer and the farmer has to pay more for his goods because we are obliged to manufacture too diversely instead of in large quantities. Furthermore, our production is not such as to give our railways a sufficient amount of business.
I think it is fair and sound reasoning that we in Canada should make ourselves not dependent rather than dependent on others, because in that way we shall build up our cities and develop our home market, and still have our export market in reserve. Therefore it is necessary that our policies should be such as to enable the farm to pay and our industries to live and in this-I see nothing incompatible or impossible, if only, instead of looking at the immediate present as we are wont to do, we turn our eyes to the near future. To dismiss an argument of that description in a few words is, of course, next to absurd.
Many things have to be done, many policies require to be adopted before our position can be altered. One of the questions which has a bearing upon our position industrially and agriculturally-and I will say with all due respect to my hon. friends of the Progressive party that I do not think they quite see how seriously it has affected them-is the question of taxation. Taxation as it exists and has existed for some time past is bound

The Address-Mr. Marler
to affect any industry or profession-and it affects industry whether it be commercial or agricultural in its character. Before the war we raised our revenue by means of customs and excise. In 1914 we raised from customs and excise $126,000,000 out of a total revenue of $136,000,000. excluding post office and railways because the revenue and the expenditure under those heads just about balanced. With that $136,000,000 we governed the country; we expended such money as was necessary, and with a very slight addition to our public debt we went our way in peace and happiness. For the period of about fourteen years before the war our public debt increased only to the extent of $67,000,000 odd, or less than $5,000,000 per year. That was all changed with the war, and instead of the old system of indirect taxation we had tax after tax imposed bj' other methods. Without doubt that taxation was necessary, and I am not at all questioning its propriety, but I am drawing a comparison between the taxation which was in vogue in this country before the war and that which was imposed subsequently. As I have said, after the war, tax after tax was imposed. We had the income tax, the business profits tax, the taxes imposed under the Special War Revenue Act; various other taxes were imposed and still prevail. In 1923 we collected $154,000,000 from customs and excise, or comparatively little more than we collected in 1914, whereas from direct taxation we collected $199,000,000. In other words, direct taxation was greater than the old indirect taxation which in the past had been in vogue.
In 1914 our total revenue from all sources was $163,000,000. In 1923 our total consolidated revenue was $394,000,000. In other words, in that ten year period taxation had increased to the extent of 225 per cent, while our population had increased in the same period by around 1,200,000 or a little over 15 per cent. That meant that a population only slightly increased had to bear an enormously increased load of taxation. And what was the effect of this taxation? There could only be one effect, nothing else could happen, any tax that is imposed, no matter how or where it is imposed or how it is collected, must be borne by one person and one person only, namely the consumer-that is where the tax eventually rests; it cannot be otherwise; there is no in-between point where that tax may land and remain; it goes on down the line until the consumer, buying his boots, shoes, farm implements or anything else, has to include it in the price he pays for the goods. So that, when taxation
like that has been imposed; where it has been necessary, in part at least, to impose it, we cannot wonder that the struggle for life has become more and more acute. We cannot wonder perhaps that our population is leaving us. We cannot wonder perhaps that some part of our population casts eyes on other countries where taxation is lighter and where the struggle for life is not so acute. But if we want prosperity in Canada we must have population; that is essential. Increase in taxation or the imposition of heavy taxation means a diminution in our population, whereas lighter taxation in any form means an increase in population.
A great deal has been said in the public press and elsewhere, even by my right hon. friend who leads the opposition-and he has been most vehement in his remarks-about the reduction of taxation. Some have stated that the taxation should be reduced by ten per cent, others twenty-five per cent, and so on. Various opinions have been given, but as a matter of fact, with all due deference to these various opinions, Mr. Speaker, they do not get us very far. They do not help us very much. They are far too general. They lack distinctiveness and definiteness in every respect. There is nothing on which one can hinge an opinion at all. I believe in spending less money; I have said so on the floor of this House time and time again. But those we have to look to as regards spending less money in this country are the people of Canada themselves, and it does not matter what this or any other government does, unless the people of Canada are willing to do without the things they have now and are willing to restrict their expenditure, taxation will never, and can never, be reduced in this country. If we are to proceed as we have proceeded certainly to some extent in years past, with everybody desiring to be government employees in this country, never in the wide world can taxation be reduced. If the provinces come forward, as they have come forward, and ask the Dominion treasury to put up money for matters that the provinces themselves should have undertaken in the past or should undertake now, then without the slightest shadow of a doubt taxation cannot be reduced. But let us turn to a happier trend of mind. We have, in so far as this government is concerned, spent less money. My hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) smiles. We have spent less money. A great deal of the money which this government had to spend was not due to its fault at all, it was the making of the hon. gentlemen who sit opposite.

The Address-Mr. Marler

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I have no objection to taking the credit for making the money.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I do not grasp the ambiguous answer which my right hon. friend has given. How has he made money for the country?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is what the hon. gentleman said. He said the money they had spent we had made. I think that is correct.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I was not clear just what he meant. No, I put it the other way. The money has been spent in matters relating to legislation which my right hon. friend and his party put through. My right hon. friend has expressed his opinion on this matter on more than one occasion. He no doubt remembers his various joumeyings in the province of Quebec. The province of Quebec was very ready and very glad to" see my right hon. friend; the city of Montreal was very glad to see him and to listen to him. He no doubt will remember the address which he made in the city of Montreal in January last, in that gilded hall, surrounded by his ex-cabinet ministers, ex-bankers, ex-shipbuilder and various others, to some of the people of Montreal. Of course, we were not all expected in that gilded chamber. The ordinary people like myself listened in from our humble homes, but unfortunately, it may sometimes be, in these modern days and the ever-present press, that which a prominent and able man like my right hon. friend says is invariably recorded and given to the world. I intend to read one or two extracts from the speech that my right hon. friend made that night. He said:
To return to expenditures, up to 1920 restriction had not been possible. But from April 1st to December 31, 1921-
That, of course, is during the fiscal year 1922.
-there had been a reduction of expenditure in ordinary revenue totalling *44,000,000. In the same period of 1922-
That is, from April 1 to December 31, 1922, being part of the fiscal year 1923.
-no reduction had taken place, but there had been an increase of approximately half a million dollars. And in the same period, 1923-
That is, from April 1 to December 31, 1923, being part of the present fiscal year, 1924.
-there had been a reduction of about $1,500,000.
Then he goes on to speak of capital expenditure and is reported in these terms:
In capital expenditure for the first nine months of the fiscal year 1921-
That is, from April 1 to December 31, 1920.

-the reduction had been $20,000,000. In the same period of 1932 the reduction had been less than $3,000,000, while last year the reduction had been less than $1,000,000.
Now, with my hon. friend's permission, let us examine somewhat in .detail that statement which he made to that well-picked crowd in Montreal which had been brought together to listen to his speech, but which the poor and humble people like myself had to listen to in another way.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It was a public meeting.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How much does a radio set cost in Montreal?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: A very small amount, but it was quite worth the amount for what we heard that night. My right hon. friend said that restriction up to 1920 had not been possible. He will correct me if I in any way inadvertently misquote him in reading from a newspaper report of his speech.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: "Reduction," I said.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is reported as "restriction", which is very much the same thing; let us use that word. Up to 1920 restriction of expenditure had not been possible, according to my right hon. friend. I suppose he meant that restriction had not been possible on account of the war. He nods his head, and I expected him to nod his head at that, because, no matter how prodigal and extravagant he was in any expenditure, in any action which was not taken that should have been taken or any action that was taken that should not have been taken, on the public hustings he always laid it to one of two causes, the war or unemployment, one or the other.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh. no; very often to the railways that my hon. friend's friends built.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: To the ones that you bought.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It will be found that in
this case my right hon. friend did not attribute the extraordinary expenditure to railways; he put it down to war and unemployment These are his two trump cards on which he relies in one case or the other as the occasion may demand. I suppose that none of these restrictions were possible at all not even in that monument of efficient bungling-the merchant marine.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No, the Liberal convention decided that it was not possible in the case of the mercantile marine.
The Address-Mr. Marler

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Liberal convention
had nothing whatsoever to do with the merchant marine. The merchant marine was a product of the brain of the government of my right hori. friend. Not one ship was put into the water except under that government. First of all, they were being built by the Imperial Munitions Board; my right hon. friend's government took the building out of the hands of the Imperial Munitions Boari' and decided to create, themselves, a great Canadian mercantile marine. That is what happened. Is the right hon. member ashamed of that policy; it was simply a mistake on the part of the government of my right hon. friend. Very well, why do they not acknowledge their mistake?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Because I differed from
that view. The hon gentleman differed from it too in 1919, because he castigated us for not building a mercantile marine for all war purposes.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am much obliged to
my right hon. friend for reminding me of what occurred in 1919. Unfortunately for my right hon. friend I was not in the House when these merchant marine estimates went through the House. Had I been in the House they would not have gone through, and my right hon. friend would not have been landed in these difficulties.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I suppose my right hon.
friend will say to me in a moment that he went into all these things with a light heart. Will he say that?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I will say what I want
to say.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Certainly. Well, I venture to say this: If my right hon. friend did go into these things with a light heart he would have been glad to have got out of them with a fleet foot.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Has the hon. gentleman
got any knowledge of what the present management of the National Railways has recommended in regard to disposing of the mercantile marine?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The railway management
recommended the acquisition of the Hotel Scribe.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
stated there had been a reduction in expenditure totalling $44,000,000. That is for the period from 1st April, to 31st December, 1921.
Why does my right hon. friend take broken periods?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Because that was the
period given in the return I asked for from the Finance department.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
What has that got to do
with it?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My right hon. friend made all the estimates for the fiscal year 1922. There is no question about that. But in any event up to the 31st March, 1922 there was not a reduction in the expenditure for that year of $44,000,000, there was a reduction of some $13,500,000, and the reduction at that time was due solely to the fact that war services had been diminished to the extent of $20,000,000 and non-war services actually increased to the extent of $6,000,000. My right hon. friend declared there had been no reduction in the fiscal year 1923. As a matter of fact there was a reduction in the fiscal year 1923 of $15,000,000.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman say that my figures were wrong in any respect?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have the return with
me that I got the figures from.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The point I want to
make, and my right hon. friend may differ with me, as this-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Answer yes or no.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have heard my right
hon. friend ask the "yes or no" question too often. That is getting to be an old story.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is quite easy for any
hon. friend to answer yes or no.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman thinks a "yes or no" answer is quite sufficient for all these purposes. He could have obtained any statement he wanted from the Finance department. Let me state that during the fiscal year to which I have reference the reduction was not $44,000,000 but was $13,-
500,000.	I repeat that the reduction for the following fiscal year was over $15,000,000. It was not the case, as my right hon. friend said, that there had been an increase of approximately half a million dollars.
The right hon. gentleman then went on to discuss capital expenditures. He said that for the first nine months of the fiscal year 1921 the reduction in capital expenditure had
The Address-Mr. Marler

been $20,000,000; and in the same period of 1922 the reduction had been less than $3,000,000; and the reduction from 1st. April to 31st., December, 1922, had been $1,000,000. Now if we go back to the year 1919 and take the fiscal years in succession, we find that the increase of 1920 over 1919 was $44,000,000. If we take the year 1921 we find there was an increase of $34,000,000 on capital and railways; and in 1922 there was a reduction of $23,000,000.
In another part of the same speech my right hon. friend said that must be done. Taxation must be reduced, the cost of departmental activities in the government must be cut, as it could be cut-the Conservatives had shown that. He says the Liberals had a chance to continue the work but had not the courage to brave the resistance and antagonism the policy had engendered. The right hon. gentleman attempts in that part of his speech to show that departmental expenditure had not been increased under his government. If he compares the departmental expenditure in 1914 with the departmental expenditure in 1922 and excludes war charges of every kind, he will find that his departmental expenditure increased to the extent of some $48,000,000 in that particular time. I can give my right hon. friend the figures.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not think you
can.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, let us have the
figures.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
What does my hon.
friend count under war expenditure?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I count under war expenditure everything relating to war.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Tell us what the expenditures are.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The accounts for 1922
show an expenditure of $347,000,000 as compared with $127,000,000 in 1914, making an increase of $220,000,000, allowing for a deduction on account of sinking fund which is not shown in 1922. We will deduct from that: War interest amounting to $108,000,000; direct services due to the war of $60,000,000; the increased subsidies to the provinces of $931,000; and special items such as unemployment relief and Dominion elections of $2,339,000; amounting in all to $171,000,000, leaving a net addition not due to the war or to special events of over $50,000,000.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not know what my hon. friend included in that item of sixty 
million dollars. He may have included only half.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, I included all the items. Would the right hon. member like the details?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Pensions; Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Soldier Settlement Board; increased cost of collection of customs, income tax and business profits tax; external affairs, various special grants, such as Patriotic Fund, League of Nations, Battlefield Memorials and grants of that kind, $60,270,396.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: There are lots besides that.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not relating to war.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, directly relating to war.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What does my right hon. friend refer to?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I would instance offhand the "Greater production" activities in the West under the Interior department.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: All that departmental increase, as a matter of fact, took place. There *were increases in every department of the government at the time. Many departments increased by many millions of dollars. I do not see what claim my right hon. friend can make in saying the departmental activities had decreased.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Many of them had increased, but what I say is that the increase was necessitated directly by the war.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How was the increase in the departments such as these necessitated by reason of the war-Agricultural Instruction Act which increased from $700,000 to $1,104,000. Was that war?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, I did not claim it was, but I observe that that was recommended to be continued by Mr. Duncan Marshall.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What has that to do with it? Then we have Experimental farms, $626,000, increased to $1,272,000; Health of Animals, $442,000 increased to $1,685,000.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I admit we were very generous to agriculture, but hon. gentlemen opposite said we were not generous enough.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is not
war.
The Address-Mr. Marler

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My right hon. friend was generous to the penitentiaries,	too-the
amount rose from $910,000 up to $1,527,000.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The inmates increased.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Bad government.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He was also generous in the cost of Civil government which increased from $5,607,000 to $9,658,000.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Did not all salaries the world over increase during the war?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: All salaries the world over certainly increased during the war. The point I make is this; that my hon. friend clearly and distinctly stated in Montreal that he had decreased governmental activities, that the Conservative party had shown how the decrease could be made. Where is that decrease?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: After the war, between 1920 and 1921, we decreased the Civil Service by over 9,000. That decrease was effected in eighteen months.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: There is not a reduction in ordinary expenditure between 1920 and 1921; there was an increase between these years.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The civil servants who were let out received their salaries, not only to the time when they went out,
4 p.m. but up to the end of 1921 and a little later. Nevertheless, the numbers diminished by over 9,000.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why is this remarkable diminution not reflected in the expenditure now?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is, but hon. gentlemen opposite are overcoming it by other expenditures.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And then after that, in the same speech, my right hon. friend went on to say that,-"War liabilities had ceased, yet the government,"-meaning the present government-"was unable to maintain the rate of reduction in expenditures".

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I said "diminish."

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
He continues
That had reflected on the cost of living which by a chart-
I am glad to see he is using charts-
-issued by the Labour department showed the jump from the imposition of the Sales Tax, the Stamp Taxes and other Liberal financial measures. The cost of living had reached its peak in 1920. It was falling rapidly in 1921 but the Mackenzie King taxes stopped the fall and there had been no reduction since.
My right hon. friend further says-
It was one of the contributory factors to emigration from Canada to the United States which in 1923 had
reached a pace truly alarming. Something must be done and done at once to stop it.
And then, in his very best form, he goes on to say-
Are we to sit by in silent, shivering impotence while these men trek right in front of our eyes into a foreign land? What must be done? Taxation must be reduced.
And later on he says-
The Sales Tax, raised from to 6 per cent, must be cut and so must other taxes.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Three per cent.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon. friend was reported to have said-and I shall be glad to send him the clipping-that it was raised from G to 6 per cent. Here it is clear and distinct. He states:
The Sales Tax raised, from 1J to 6 per cent must be cut, and so must other taxes.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I said G and 14, it
being divided. Hon. gentlemen laugh, but I do not think they understand this yet. If hon. members do not want the matter cleared they do not need to have it cleared. I usually in my speeches refer to our Sales Tax as G and 11, totalling 3, because we divide the expense of collection, but I never represented that it was li to any audience in Canada.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, that is what the
listeners heard, or what they believed they heard.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. member did not get it over the radio.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The expression was perfectly clear and distinct in the city of Montreal that the Sales Tax had been raised from li to 6 per cent.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They all know better than that in Montreal.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: However, that statement remains. It has been reported, and reported on more than one occasion, and has never been contradicted by my right hon. friend to my knowledge.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I did not read it. I knew I made the correct statement, and that satisfied me.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Why does my hon. friend
say that war expenditure had ceased in 1920?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I did not say it. I said it diminished.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Could these "asides" be rendered in a little louder voice, so that we in this part of the chamber might have the full benefit of it?

The Address-Mr. Marler

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Might I suggest to hon. members on. both sides that, in a debate of this nature, it would be wise for hon. members to stop the interruptions and the crossexamination. I say it without any invidious meaning towards anyone in particular, but I think that for the dignity of the House the debate should proceed without interruption. Unless the hon. member interrupting addresses himself to the Chair on a question of order, or unless the hon. member who has the floor is inviting cross-examination, there should be no interruption.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I explain, Mr. Speaker? The invitation came very directly, . from the hon. gentleman, as he admits, and I admire him for it. If he would prefer it, I am quite prepared to be silent, and, except in a special case, I will not interrupt him at all.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am much obliged to you, Mr. Speaker, for the courtesy and kindness in making this suggestion. I have no particular objection to the interruptions of my right hon. friend. The point I am trying to accomplish is to have the truth known throughout the country, as to what the government has done and what they have attempted to do, and as to the burden they have had saddled on their backs since they came into power, and their inability to make any further reductions than have been made. When a prominent statesman like my right hon. friend comes to an important city like Montreal and makes these statements, which are heralded abroad in the public press-as a matter of fact they were spread broadcast in the constituency I represent-it is obvious that they must be corrected somewhere; and when I undertake to correct them I do so, not necessarily with the object of annoying or exciting my right hon. friend at all, that is not my purpose, but simply to get to the actual truth of the facts. We . are only trying to have reported in the newspapers exactly what did1 happen, exactly what was done.
I trust you will overlook the digression, Mr. Speaker. My right hon. friend attempted in that speech to make it distinct beyond any misunderstanding that, notwithstanding the war and demobilization, the expenditure on the part of his government had diminished, and diminished very considerably. I do not think I misread his remarks in that respect. Very well. In the fiscal year 1920 the total expenditure, less war and demobilization, was in round numbers, 1439,000,000; for the fiscal year 1921 the total expenditure, less war and
[Mr. McMaster.l
demobilization, was $511,000,000, an increase of $72,000,000. For the year 1922, again comparing it with the year 1920, the total expenditure, less war and demobilization, was $462,000,000, an increase as compared with 1920, of $22,800,000. In 1923 the total expenditure, less war and demobilization,-and that was the first year that this government had an opportunity of making reductions-was $429,000,000, or a considerable reduction as compared with 1920. What was the result of the reduction which this government made? I admit that in 1923 the demobilization expenditure was small, but I have deducted war and demobilization expenditure from the other years as well so as to put the accounts on an equal basis and make a fair comparison. The reduction which this government made in 1923, as compared with the year 1920, was $9,269,000, while it was $81,000,000 less than in 1921 and $32,000,000 less than in 1922. These are the reductions which this government has made. I might add, for the benefit of my right hon. friend and of hon. members generally, that in the expenditure of 1923 there is an amount of about $6.000,000-to be exact, $5,979,000 -for the merchant marine and another $5,000,000 for the Canada Highways Act, with which this government had absolutely nothing in the world to do. That would have made the net deficit in that year only $15,000,000. Now let me take the deficits that occurred during these years, because I want to lead up to the question of taxation and as to whether we can reduce those taxes or not. The deficits for the years 1920, 1921 and 1922, that is to say, the total deficits, amounted to $609,000,000. And yet, notwithstanding all this, my right hon. friend comes forward and declares that taxation must be reduced. He says that the Liberal government imposed taxes which they should not have imposed. Will my right hon. friend tell me how he expected the interest on the deficits to be paid? Was it to be paid out of the earnings of the merchant marine or out of those of the railways?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
want an answer?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I should prefer to leave
out the Belle river and Matane wharves, and hotels and other things. If that were done there would be no necessity to increase the taxes.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is not the point in question, nor is it the point I make. I am referring to an allegation, clear and distinct, which my hon. friend made without the

The Address-Mr. Marler
slightest ambiguity in the city of Montreal, to the effect that we imposed unnecessary taxes. He said that we imposed taxes. Of course we did: what else could be done but impose additional taxes? Were those deficits that were occurring year after year to be allowed to continue? Were they to be pyramided? Had we allowed that sort of thing to go on we should have reached the stage where further progress would have been impossible. As a matter of fact we had reached that stage in my right hon. friend's administration although he never thought that we had. He did not want to impose additional taxation; he saw looming up in the future another matter of greater importance, the election, and consequently he said, " No, I will not impose taxes." My right hon. friend is perfectly well aware that the taxes he imposed in the war did not even cover the interest on war expenditures. Does he deny that?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Did not cover war expenditures?-Certainly not. Did any country in the world do that?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
knows quite well what I mean: it did not cover the interest on war expenditure and had nothing to do with war capital. The war capital is absolutely intact at the present time, $1,693,000,000, with a deficit in addition to that. And yet here is a statement made by my right hon. friend as appears in the Border City Star:
Regarding the assertion of Premier King in his recent speech at Quebec, that the former federal government had paid nothing in the way of war debts out of taxes, Mr. Meighen flatly charges this to be a falsehood. In 1919 Great Britain had paid 27 per cent of the war cost out of taxation in addition to meeting normal current expenditures, Mr. Meighen said. Canada had actually done better with a record of 28 per cent.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is right too.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Is the hon. gentlemaD serious?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, sir.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My right hon. friend still persists in saying that part of the war capital expenditure was paid by his government.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I said just what my hon. friend read, that 28 per cent of all war costs was paid by the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Capital cost?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What does the statement mean?	*

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It means what it says. I am ready to stay with the hon. member to
n
the end, if he will. It means exactly what it says, 28 per cent of all war costs.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Very well. That is an interesting statement and I want to get the matter in Hansard; I want it to go throughout the country; I want the House to know exactly the position which the late government took in imposing war taxes on the country, so that there will be no question about the situation at all. Of course, we all know that the late government won the war; we have been told that in the province of Quebec time and again. In regard to taxation which is put on binders, harrows and ploughs, the right hon. gentleman opposite need not look to Brantford when he talks about costs; let him look to the right. That is where the expenditure came from. However, my right hon. friend not only did not pay-and I make the statement advisedly and with care-one single dollar on war capital out of war taxes, but in addition to that, on the first of April, 1922, that is to say at the end of the fiscal year 1921, there was a deficit in connection with actual interest, pensions and war services of $128,000,000. I shall give my right hon. friend the figures. That is precisely what he saddled this government and the country with. I am not blaming him for these war expenditures, don't let him misunderstand me.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman give details?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
With the greatest
pleasure. I worked out these figures this morning with the published statistics, to be quite. sure of their correctness. With permission I will read the table:

I do not think there can be any question whatever that when this government took charge there was this deficit of $128,191,344 as regards ordinary, everyday war expenditure, to say nothing of capital expenditure.
But Mr. Speaker, the sad feature of the situation is that when the opportunity was before this country of imposing taxes upon those who were making millions out of the war such taxes were not then imposed. Of course, hon. gentlemen on this side of the House are well aware why the opportunity was ignored-an election was in the offing. Hence, instead of imposing taxes those who were rich were made richer, for instead of issuing war bonds subject to tax, which my right hon. friend had a perfect right to do- he could do anything under the War Measures Act; he could have even taken all the money out of the banks-he issued tax-free bonds. Of course the cry will go up from him and his associates: "We had to work up great enthusiasm in order to get the people to buy war bonds." But these bonds are the very best investment in the country. However, he issued $915,000,000 of non-taxable war bonds- at least, that is the amount still outstanding.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman know of any belligerent country that did not take that course?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Such a question is simply the product of a vivid imagination-nothing more, nothing less. It is not a question of what this or that country did. He has been telling us on this side of the House that we have imposed more taxes. He came down to the city of Montreal and said:	Taxes must
be reduced. It is he who came forward to lead us to believe, rightly or wrongly-and perhaps wrongly-that our sales tax was raised from li to 6 per cent by this government. That is what the people were led to believe by his speech in Montreal. I am controverting that statement absolutely. I say this government did the only possible thing-they imposed additional taxation. They did not want to do so; what interest was it to this government to impose additional taxation? But even the war interest was not

met by my right hon. friend by taxing those who were making millions out of the war.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt the hon. gentleman, and I will not if he asks me to refrain, but does he know of any business profits tax in any country in the world higher than Canada's was? That tax was imposed on the people he refers to, and if he thinks it was not enough why doesn't he restore and augment it?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I know of no business
profits tax that was as high as Canada's. I know of no business profits tax in any other country; but what I know, and what every hon. member knows, is that millions and millions of dollars were made during the war in a manner that should not have been possible and those profits should have been returned to the people. I know, further, that $915,000,000 of non-taxable bonds are outstanding. The interest on these alone, $45,000,000 is paying no income tax, which means that these gentlemen across the way are paying so much more income tax themselves. That is the fact, and that is what we are complaining of. And yet my right hon. friend says: "Are we to sit by in silent, shivering impotence?" Well, my right hon. friend did not sit by "in silent, shivering impotence" when immigration went dead; he sat by in frozen inactivity. I observe that my right hon. friend is producing some figures, and I know what they are; he has read them half a dozen times in the House already.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, he has not read them at all. Would my hon. friend like to hear them?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Well, let us hear what my right hon. friend has to say about them now.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I knew that the Minister of Customs would commence to roar, but I do not rise unless I have the backing. The official figures show. . .

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. This is the seventy-eighth speech that my right hon. friend has made. Seventy-five is enough.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Marler) invited me to give the figures.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Do I understand that the hon. member who has the floor gave his permission to the right hon. leader of the opposition to interrupt?

The Address-Mr. Marler

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I again say, Mr. Speaker, that I have no objection to the hon. member's interruptions.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Well, we have.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I really do not like to interrupt him so often, but there is not a sentence he has uttered that I would not like to have contradicted, and of that contradiction to have produced the proof. I have before me the emigration and immigration figures from the official records. At the beginning of the war and for many years prior to that time the balance was strongly in our favour. At the very opening of the war the balance went heavily against us, until about February, 1917 -I will give the exact figures if hon. gentlemen want me to. We could not impose higher taxation. The Americans were not in the war, and higher taxation-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Higher taxation would
have made a higher balance against us. On the entrance of the American nation into the war our taxation reached a level the highest in the world, and immigration started in our favour and continued in our favour.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The balance continued
heavily in our favour every year until September, '1922. It has been heavily against us ever since.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: With regard to the point of order raised by the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau), I do not think the right hon. leader of the opposition has the right to make speeches over and over again. He might put questions, but he should not speak every day on the same subject. He has exhausted his right to speak.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have already stated to the House that this cross-examining process is against the rules. Unless the hon. member who has the floor allows the interruption to take place and the explanation to be given, he must proceed with his speech. Here is the rule:
Whilst a member is addressing the House no one has a right to interrupt him by putting a question to him, or by making or demanding an explanation. A member will at times allow such interruptions through a sense of courtesy to another but it is entirely at the option of the member in possession of the floor to give way or not to an immediate explanation.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We do not know at the
present time wTho has the floor, whether it is the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) or the member for St Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler).

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, these interruptions
are only wearying the House, and perhaps hon. members will be very glad when I sit down.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, go on.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My right hon. friend, in
the address he made a few minutes ago, stated that he could controvert or repudiate most of the statements I have made.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
He can repudiate them
all?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: In about five minutes.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I will let my hon. friend
repudiate the statement that there was a deficit in actual war expenditure as compared with everyday expenditure.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I do now.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Of course he can do it
now; that is exactly the attitude he took in Montreal in saying that taxes should be reduced-but it is nothing but noise; there is nothing in it at all. We are looking for reasons in this country now; we do not propose to sit under taxation without knowing the reason. We are more or leas intelligent people in Montreal. I am not saying that the body before which my right hon. friend spoke was as intelligent as some of the others, but still a fairly intelligent body. My right hon. friend, in his best style, ended up his address by saying, "Are we going to sit by in silent, shivering impotence while our people trek across the line to the United States?" I was going on to say a few moments ago, when my right hon. friend interjected his address, that he not only stood by "in silent, shivering impotence" as regards immigration; he stood by in frozen inactivity. The department itself was frozen and an encumbrance on the government. It was known in the United States, through reports of depar-mental officials, that it was the most difficult thing in the wide world to gain entrance into Canada under the rules which were enforced at that time. Here is a paragraph from one of those reports; it is a comment by Mr. W. J. White, Superintendent of Agencies in the United States:
During the war period, drastic restrictions were necessarily put into effect, and no doubt for good reasons these were continued after the close of the war. While they had the desired effect of keeping out many undesirables, the precautions were so sweeping that there were those who, able to qualify as far as farming experience, character, finances, etc., were denied admission, owing to the legal obstructions that it was not deemed advisable to remove.
The Address-Mr. Marler

Then it goes on to state the difficulties, and finally ends up by saying:
It could not be overtaken. In fact, everywhere there was an almost general impression that admission to Canada was so difficult as to be almost impossible.
Now, immigration is not a thing that you can turn on like a water tap from which you get so many buckets of water, and then turn off. The machinery of immigration went dead, frozen, silent, under the administration of my right hen. friend. He deliberately put upon the shores of this country a sign that none need apply; that was the effect, at least, The offices on the continent were closed- and that is what happened as regards immigration.
I want again to call attention to what my right hon. friend said as regards the sales tax. The statement he made will be clearly and distinctly corrected in Hansard and clearly and distinctly corrected in the press, so that the poorer classes in the city of Montreal who had not the privilege of attending that meeting will know that the cost of their food was not raised by six per cent, as they were led to believe, but that the tax in 1923 was actually less instead of greater than that of 1922. As a matter of fact, under the new law-and I am free to admit that I do not like the new law very well, but that is neither here nor there-the tax was lessened when compared with that imposed in 1922. Hon. gentlemen are aware of how the sales tax was imposed. It came into effect in 1920, and in that year it was imposed on two steps of trade only, that is, manufacturer to wholesaler, and wholesaler to retailer. In 1921 it was imposed on the three steps of trade, that is, producer to manufacturer, manufacturer to wholesaler, and wholesaler to retailer. That tax as originally imposed was one per cent on the ordinary channels of trade. The Conservative government raised that tax 50 per cent on the ordinary channels of trade, and this government when it came into office in 1922 raised it another 50 per cent. In other words, on each of the three steps of the ordinary channels of trade the tax was 2i per cent. Under the 1923 law the tax was not raised but was placed on one step and one step only, that is to say,. 6 per cent on all three steps combined. But the ordinary man in the street will want to know exactly what this means. He does not understand these figures. He thinks when he hears on the public hustings that the tax has been raised from one-and-a-half to six per cent that everything he buys at the comer grocery store and everywhere else, every suit of clothes and every pair of boots and shoes that he buys, 
has six per cent added to that particular purchase. That is the impression that has gone abroad, and that impression is totally and absolutely incorrect. We will take for example, $1,000 worth of raw material and see what it costs manufactured into the finished article under each of these laws, and what the tax is to be paid under each law. Under the law of 1920 the total tax was $51.92, and the cost of goods to the consumer was $3,544.05. In 1921 the tax was $88.99, and the cost of the finished article to the consumer $3,648.06. In 1922 the tax was $119.60, and the cost to the consumer $3,714.16. In 1923 the tax is $111.01, and the cost to the consumer $3,676.46. Now let us get clearly and distinctly in our minds what the cost of goods under the law of 1923 was over the cost under the law of 1921. It was $28.40, or slightly over three-quarters of one per cent-not six per cent-and when the law of 1923 was put into effect there was a reduction of $37.77, or over one per cent. That, of course, as hon. members will understand, is simply in the ordinary channels of trade There were under the old act various matters which meant that the tax could be very much increased.
I must apologize for taking up so much of the time of the House, but I fear that I have a great deal more to say. I was starting out to ask a few_ moments ago, before I had the delightful digression with my right hon. friend across the way which we both enjoyed so much, whether we could reduce taxation in this country or not. I do not think there is any use anybody saying we must reduce taxes, or that we must reduce taxation by a certain percentage or in a certain way, until we first examine what our requirements and what our revenues are, for that, after all, is the true test of the situation.
What are our requirements? Our requirements are, of course, firstly to pay the interest on our war debt, to pay for our war services, and, if possible, to create a sinking fund for the purpose of paying off our war liabilities; secondly, to pay our ordinary requirements, that is, our non-war debt, our subsidies to the provinces, and the various, everyday, out-ofpocket requirements; and thirdly, to pay our railway debt to keep our railways alive. Before taking up what revenues we have to meet these requirements, there is one matter which I would most respectfully place before the Minister of Finance, and it is this: Why do we not in this country divide our war taxes into one separate group with our war expenditure, and put our ordinary taxes into another group with our ordinary expenditure?
The Address-Mr. Marler

As it is at the present time, the taxes imposed for war and the taxes imposed for ordinary purposes are all put in precisely the same account, and although war taxes are reasonably borne, nevertheless it seems to me unfair, it seems to create an ambiguity, it seems to create more or less deception to ask people to pay war taxes that are not to be used for war purposes at all. As a matter of fact should not our war taxes be used for war purposes, and if there is a surplus of war taxes should not that surplus be used in the reduction of our debt and for a sinking fund? And if we have too much of a surplus as regards our war taxes, why should not our war taxes as such be reduced?
Then we come to ordinary taxation, which fills the next category. Should we not try and bring our ordinary expenditure within the four comers of our ordinary taxes? That is to say, segregate our ordinary taxes for ordinary, evervday purposes?
Then we come to the third category, the railways. We no doubt have to keep our railways alive but it seems to me if we want money for our railways we should call our railway expenditure a railway tax or a tax of that description. In other words if that system were followed out there would be no ambiguity, no deception. Everybody would know exactly what they were paying for and exactly what they were getting. Now I come to the question whether we could reduce the taxes. Let us take the figures for the year 1923, and they are of very considerable interest. Take, first of all, the war expenditure. The war revenue on Consolidated Fund was $199,732,496, and on special account something over $8,000,000 odd, or a total war revenue of $207,000,000.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
What does the hon.
member characterize as war revenue?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I will give the details of
that with pleasure. They are as follows:
Customs and	sales	tax, etc	 $106,482,000
Income	 59,711,000
Business profits		13,031,000
Miscellaneous,	Finance Dept	 2,409,000
Interest on advances to foreign governments	 10,000,000
Post Office	 7,000,000
Then there are various subsidiary amounts from the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment and the Soldiers' Settlement Board amounting to $1,000,000, which gives us a total of $199,732,496, plus an amount from special account of $8,199,000, which is a particular amount for exchange received from the British government last year. That makes a total of $207,931,829.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
What part of customs
does the hon. member allocate as being war revenue? I am merely asking for information.
I think we are all immensely interested in this analysis of our financial situation and the hon. member has stated that certain moneys coming through the custom house are to be regarded as war revenue. Just what revenue coming through the custom house is to be regarded as war revenue and why?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend will understand, it is taxation collected through the customs department. It also includes a certain amount derived from the sales tax.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And imposed in consequence of the war?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Imposed, in consequence of the war.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It includes excise taxes?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Excise taxes,' sales tax,
taxes of that description. Perhaps I shouid have said that was the mode of collection. It has nothing to do with customs duty at all; it is kept separate entirely.
Then we had our expenditure for war purposes. There was interest on the war debt of $108,000,000. That amount is a rather complicated one to make up, but I have had it verified by the Bureau of Statistics. There is also war services and incidental services, $52,699,000, and there were demobilization charges that year of $4,000,000, making a total expenditure of $165,000,000, leaving a surplus from war taxes of $42,767,945. Hon. members will understand that the point I am trying to make-these figures naturally intervene in any discourse in a matter of this description-is whether it is possible at the present time to reduce the taxation, and my claim is that as regards war taxes, in view of these surpluses, it would be possible to reduce in so far as the war taxes themselves are concerned.
Then coming down to our ordinary revenue, our total revenue for ordinary and special account amounted to $195,000,000, and our expenditure on ordinary and special account amounts to $175,000,000. As against that, should be deducted some $5,000,000 on government railway account, leaving a surplus of $25,000,000. Consequently from these two sources, war account and ordinary account, our finances show a surplus on all accounts of $68,000,000. Now, one would imagine on hearing of a surplus of that description that it would be possible to reduce the taxation. That would be possible if the railway situation
The Address-Mr. Marler

had not to be taken into account. When we consider the railway situation not only is this surplus eaten up, but $22,000,000 in addition. During the year 1923 the cost of our railways-all	the government railwaysamounted to $84,960,037, and the cost of our merchant marine amounted to $5,979,000, or a total expenditure on railways and ships of $90,939,000. Consequently our war surplus to the extent of $43,000,000 was used for the purpose of keeping alive our railways and our ships; also the additional surplus we had from ordinary account, plus $22,000,000 as well. With these figures before us one can ask himself if it is possible to reduce taxation. Of course taxation could be reduced if we were to write up all our expenditure to capital account, but that would mean making deficit after deficit and the day of reckoning would very soon arrive. As a matter of fact the position of affairs is that our surplus from war expenditure and our surplus from ordinary expenditure are being used to keep our railway situation alive at the present time.	[DOT]

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why not get clear of the railways?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
This year it is stated that the railways will show an operating surplus of some $20,000,000, which is very much better than the operating surplus of some $4,000,000 last year, and the inference might be drawn that our railways are at last commencing to pay. But that is not the case at all. It is not a question merely of operating surplus. There are many other charges, as regards the railways, which must be taken into account- such as construction betterments, repayment, of old loans, extensions, and various other expenditures of that description, to say nothing of interest to the public, and leaving out of consideration entirely interest to the government. The true test, Mr. Speaker, as regards the railways, and as regards taxation relative to the railways, is, not what the operating deficit or what the operating profit may be, but it is what the public treasury must put up every year to keep these railways alive. That is the situation which should I think be understood by every member of the House. We read in the newspapers from time to time that the operating profit of the government railways is so much more this year than last year, but there are many other expenditures which must be taken into account. Take for example: In 1920 the loss on railway operation was $32,503,000 but we paid out of the public treasury on railway account $123,000,000. In 1921 the loss on railway operation

was $11,847,000, while we paid out of the pub-lie treasury $105,000,000. In 1922 there was an operating profit of $4,193,000, and yet we paid out of the public treasury $84,000,000. Even if the operating surplus in 1923 amounts to $20,000,000 I think hon. gentlemen will find that there will have to be in the public accounts this year probably fifty or sixty million dollars still to keep these railways alive.
Now, there are various opinions in this House as regards the question of government owned railways. Some of us say that the railways should not have been taken over; others think that they should have been taken over. Some think that these railways are a great national asset; others think they are a great national liability. I admit quite freely that it will serve no good purpose to discuss these questions at the present time; we are perhaps past that stage. Personally I have always said, and I must state again on the floor of the House, that I do not see any particular advantage in public ownership of railways. Public ownership to me shows many disadvantages. Public ownership does not mean that railway rates are lessened in the very slightest degree.
The owners of a railway do not lessen railway rates. The owners perhaps are contributory factors in having railway rates high or low on account of efficiency or inefficiency. More efficient management may tend to lower the rates because there is a greater profit, but the main fact we have got to consider is that a railway must get a sufficient amount of traffic to keep it alive, and even a reduction or writing down of its capital cost is not going to help in the very least. Of course the protagonists of public ownership will say to me "We should keep these railways under public ownership." I fear that I must answer for myself in substantially the same way that I did when my right hon. friend first put to me a question two years ago-I personally prefer to see these railways in the hands of private individuals and administered by a private body.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why have we got public ownership at this time?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: To answer my hon. friend's question would tax too much the patience of the House-it is a very long story.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Because the government
took them over.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would like to ask my hon. friend, when he denounces the public ownership of railways does he not

The Address-Mr. Marler
know that private ownership of railways in the United States has reached an absolute state of bankruptcy?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We are dealing with Canada.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The freight rates are higher than ours.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I regret that I cannot
answer the question of my hon. friend in an efficient manner. However, the question whether public ownership or private ownership is good, bad or indifferent is hardly a question to discuss at this time; but I would like to say to those who believe in public ownership that vast sums of money have been spent on these railways. Since 1920 we have paid out of the public treasury $392,000,000 for the purpose of these railroads. That is entirely outside of interest on many millions that had previously been put into these railways, and a great many more millions which does not appear in this amount at all.
