Therefore, I say to those hon. gentlemen who ask for lines to be extended and for various other matters to be effected, that they should have a little consideration for those who do not believe in public ownership quite as much as they do. In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, I think that the financing of the railways is far too easy a matter. The public treasury is far too open, and easy money always encourages extravagance in any matter of that description. We have heard the cry time and time again in this House and out of the House that the railways should be kept out of politics. At the same time we hear the cry shouted lustily "But we will hold you responsible for our funds;" That is what the people say. Those two cries are entirely and totally incompatible. The railways cannot be kept out of politics. They should not be kept out of politics, so long as they are owned by the government, and every dollar spent on railways should come before the House and be voted upon in a most careful and meticulous way. As a matter of fact, we cannot hide behind the cry that we should keep the railways out of politics, and unless we take every possible thing into consideration in voting the amount of money in question, it seems to me we are very failing in our trust. The practical solution of the matter of these lines, whether they are in the hands of the public or in the hands of private individuals, is to have more traffic east and west on the railways, and for that we need more production. We need people and more consumption in our country, and to obtain that consumption and production implies not only
more immigration but it implies also less emigration. Therefore how can we arrive at a solution to have less emigration from the country. My answer to that is that we are not sufficiently self-reliant and selfdependent in this country. We depend upon others to do for us what we should 5 p.m. do for ourselves. We import far too much manufactured goods and far too much foodstuffs. We should grow or manufacture these things ourselves. We should buy the foodstuffs from our own farmers. We should manufacture in this country what we can manufacture, and what we cannot manufacture we should learn to manufacture. In other words, we should be a self-dependent Canadian nation. I do not think we are a self-dependent nation. At the very least, and without the slightest exaggeration, during the calendar year 1923 we imported into this country no less than fifty million dollars worth of foodstuffs which could have been grown in this country and the money kept in this country and given to the farmers, just as well as to anybody else. In the same period of time, without the slightest semblance of exaggeration, we imported into the country one hundred and fifty million dollars' worth of manufactured goods which we could have manufactured here, which would have made work for our population in this country, and kept our money here. We look for our trade to the United States. We say to the United States "We will buy a large amount from you," and we did import from the United States last year in the neighbourhood of fifty million dollars' worth of foodstuffs, and the United States said to us in the year 1921, under the Fordney Tariff, "We do not want to have anything to do with you, get out." And under the Fordney and Mc-Cumber Tariff of 1922 they slammed and locked the door in our faces. That is the position the United States has taken as regards trading with us. But notwithstanding that our exports to the United States have fallen from 52 per cent in 1868 to 39 per cent in 1923, and our imports have risen from 33 per cent in 1868 to 67 per cent in 1923. As a matter of fact last year we bought from the States $200,000,000 more than the United States bought from us, and our exports to the United States, would show much less, if it were not the fact that we export a great deal of unmanufactured wood and a great deal of pulp and paper. In other words, I claim that we are buying from the United States a great many things we could grow on our own farms and make in our own factories. That would give employment to our people and keep in circulation the money of this country in Canada.
The Address-Mr. Marler

Then again take another situation. In 1897 we made with Great Britain what we called a reciprocal tarig. In 1898 we converted that into a preferential tarig. We increased that preferential tarig in 1900, and again in 1922 and again in 1923, and why did we do all this? We did this no doubt mainly in the hope that we would increase our exports to Great Britain, and although we have never said so, perhaps in the hope that some day Great Britain would give us a like preference as regards our staple products over the same products imported by it from other parts, outside of the Empire. We never said that or hinted it, but we hoped it would come. If we did all this for the purpose of increasing our exports, it has been a most dismal failure, because our exports to Great Britain have diminished from 56 per cent to just about 40 per cent and our imports have also diminished from 27 per cent in 1897 to 17 per cent in 1923, but during the period from 1897 to 1923 we became a much greater manufacturing country. During the war, in part to help the Mother Country, we built factories here, and, therefore that meant that those factories had to be kept busy and workmen had to be employed in those self-same factories. But notwithstanding that, and notwithstanding the fact that labour in Great Britain is paid a great deal less, we say to Great Britain, " Come along and take part of our market." It does not seem to me that that is a rational attitude to take at the present time.
In addition to that, there is the serious question of depreciated currency which must be taken into consideration. There is the question of depreciated currency from countries on the continent. Many goods come in under the British preferential tarig that are not entirely British made goods. As a matter of fact, British made goods under the British preferential tarig only have to be fabricated in England to the extent of 25 per cent, and the other 75 per cent is just as likely to be fabricated on the continent by cheap labour, and yet they are imported into Canada under the British preferential tarig, and those goods come in here and take the place of goods which we ourselves could make in this country. And then we invite other countries on the continent who have depreciated currencies to come in and take a part of our markets, too. I do not consider such a situation rational at all. I know quite well that there may be some gentlemen in this House who will wholly or at least in part disagree with me on this momentous subject. My hon. 
friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) and many other hon. gentlemen across the goor who may be inclined to think so, need not for a moment assume that I am what is called a high and rabid protectionist; I am not; I do not speak for any manufacturer or any group of manufacturers; I have no personal interest to urge in that respect at all. I do ask, not for a tarig to pay high dividends; not for a tarig to help those who are not capable; not for a tarig to pay any dividends on watered stock. What I do ask for is "a cost-of-living tarig" which will enable our industries to exist and provide labour for our workmen in order that we may build up our cities and increase interior production, and make our railways pay their way. I do not think that such an attitude is at all unreasonable. For that reason I ask that the tarig be inquired into by those competent to make that inquiry, and that upon the advice so obtained the tarig be adjusted in a fair and reasonable manner. Until that is done I ask that no changes in the tarig, the egect of which are not understood or which may be inadvisable, be made.
I would remind the House that there is an urgent need for inquiry in reference to some of our industries the conditions of which merit investigation. It is said by some that a wrong has been done them. If a wrong has been done, is it unreasonable to ask that it be inquired into and, if wrong exists, that that wrong be removed? I appreciate the fact that in reference to the tarig there are many hon. gentlemen who will say that they care nothing about "a cost-of-living tarig," about "a development tarig," or about the Canadian manufacturer. With all deference to these gentlemen I say:	Deny the principle of a
cost-of-living tarig and you will close our industries and create greater depression; more than that, you will prevent many industries which barely exist to-day, from paying the taxes which are necessary for the administration of the agairs of the country and which are required to keep the railways alive and, perhaps in better times, to extend those railways. That is what will happen if the tarig is reduced in any inadvisable manner the egect of which is not sufficiently understood.
I have always been perfectly frank so far as my attitude to the tarig is concerned; I have never been ambiguous in my views on the fioor of the House. I am not one who is not ready to concede changes in matters of policy provided I am shown a good and sufficient reason for those changes. I take the same stand now in relation to the tariff as I took on the floor of this House two years

The Address-Mr. Marler
ago, and in the country as well, when I was elected on the principles I then advocated. I do not regard the tariff as a dogma which cannot be altered. It requires changes from time to time necessitating readjustments, and in my opinion it should be framed in the interests of revenue and in the interests of the honest, the decent and the efficient manufacturer. I do not for a single moment advocate a tariff in the interests of the man who makes vast sums in the way of dividends, not at all; what I ask for is a tariff that will provide a living wage for our workmen and will keep our people in the country. I have also stated that the tariff should be framed in the light of expert advice. I stated two years ago, as I state now, that I believed in the Laurier-Fielding tariff. That tariff brought prosperity to this country, and in the years from 1896 to 1911 very little was heard about tariff matters at all. Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier himself as well as other Liberal leaders gave utterance to sentiments very largely in accordance with those I am expressing today on this important subject. If hon. gentlemen will bear with me, I will read the following words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier which have been quoted before in this House. This matter is one of importance equally alike to hon. gentlemen opposite and to myself. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
It is a humiliating confession to make that after three centuries of existence this country is still unable to supply its own wants and that it is still obliged to have recourse to foreign markets, though nature has lavished upon it all the gifts necessary to render it a manufacturing country. . . It is the duty especially for us Canadians of French origin to create. . . Thus far it seems to me that the government has been moving in the wrong direction. The government has devoted itself to recruiting an exclusively agricultural immigration; its efforts will end in nothing-the agricultural population of this country will never be increased from outside. . . We can, however,-
And this is the point I wish to stress.
-introduce here with good results, I think, an industrial immigration. I do not mean simple workmen, but master mechanics and small capitalists, such as are to be found in all the cities of Europe.
Later on another gentleman expressed the following views, which I think will be recognized :
We do not propose to do anything that will interfere with legitimate business. We do not propose to do anything that will interfere with legitimate profits, nor, much less, do we propose to do anything that would injure our industries in any fair competition with the industries of other countries. We realize that Canada, if she is to be great, must be a country based on diversified industries. This is the day of world competition, not between town and town, or factory and factory, but between continent and continent, and realizing that, we do not propose to take steps that are in any way going to check the nation's just industries in carrying on their business in a just and reasonable way.
I do not think that my attitude to the tariff is at all different from that. No doubt someone will say that this is not a country which should rest upon a basis of diversified industries. Some gentlemen possibly might say: "Let us buy our boots and shoes in Boston instead of from the province of Quebec; let us buy our cottons and woollens from England instead of in Ontario; let us import our window glass from Belgium and our oilcloths from Germany", and so on. There are those who will say, "It does not matter whether these things are made by Canadian workmen or made by foreigners, and if they are cheaper elsewhere, we should buy them in the cheaper market. It matters not that we have attempted to build up a market in Canada during so many years. There are people who will be indifferent as to whether we preserve that market for our own producers or for someone else.
Now, I do not deny for one moment that, owing to the peculiar circumstances of the times, we can to-day bring in from these countries commodities at a lower price than they can be manufactured here. But my point is this: Are we going to build up Canada for the immediate present, or are we going to look some little way into the future? Are we to keep only the present in our vision, or are we to look further ahead to the needs of our population, not only the population here now but the population which we hope will come in the future? If we view the present only, all we have to do is continue as we are doing, converting this country into a warehouse and a dumping ground. If, on the other hand, we have vision and patience and look towards the future building-up of this country, allowing our factories to work at fuli time instead of half time, then the cost of commodities will be decreased, because factories on full time must necessarily produce at a far less expense than when operating at half time, as is the case to-day. In addition to that, although foreign goods are now being brought in at a lower price than similar goods can be produced by our own manufacturers, when conditions become stabilized in Europe and exchange becomes again normal, those very goods will cost substantially as much as we ourselves, in course of time, will be able to manufacture them. But we will never be in this position industrially if inadvisable and illthought-out changes are made in the tariff. I do not suggest that, such changes would be made in a vicious spirit, I accuse no one of any such desire; but if changes are
The Address-Mr. Marler

made without their probable effects being very fully considered,' -our towns and cities will be bound to disappear. But we must also take into consideration-and I think the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) made a point of this the other day-that if we reduce these centres to stagnation, to a very large extent we reduce our home market. This should be our first market to look to, and our export market should be the next.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Has the home market helped the American agriculturist to any appreciable extent? Is he any better off to-day than the Canadian agriculturist?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: With all due deference to my hon. friend, I submit that the home market has without a doubt helped our agriculturists, and without the home market they could not have got rid of the same amount of their products.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What part of his product could the Canadian farmer not have got rid of?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I will explain in a moment to my hon. friend just what the Canadian agriculturist has got rid of in his home market.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That does not necessarily mean that he could not have got rid of it. The consumption of wheat in Europe to-day is only one-third of the normal consumption.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend could have got rid of more wheat than was got rid of by means of the export trade. Our wheat was exported to the. fullest extent possible.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: To all the extent that was necessary.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: But all of the wheat grown was not exported.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: TheTe was no need to export it.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Perhaps I may be quite ignorant, but this is the way it appeals to me. In the crop year 1921-22 we produced around
300.000,000 bushels of wheat. Of this, 194,000,000 bushels was exported as wheat and flour, and 106,000,000 bushels was consumed in Canada. The latter was worth at least $85,000,000. In addition, there were the byproducts which we retained. I apologize, Mr. Speaker, for taking up so much of the time of the House.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Go ahead.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We cannot export wheat and flour alone.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not without purchasing other commodities; I agree with you there.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Not without exporting
other commodities.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not without importing other commodities; trade cannot be one-sided.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend will pardon me for contradicting him. I do not think we can establish trade channels in wheat and flour alone; we must export other commodities also.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would my hon. friend expect any country to take nothing but wheat and flour from us? Would he expect a ship to be loaded with wheat and flour only? No ship will go out with such a cargo.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why not?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: To create a general trade we have to carry various products to other countries.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What will it bring back in return?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is precisely the point I make with my hon. friend from Swift Current. It creates trade; but our customers overseas will not say to us that they want only our wheat and flour. It is necessary and essential for trade routes to be made up by exporting other commodities besides wheat and flour in order to create in the foreign port the needed market for our wheat and flour, because the more trade we have with any country the more demand there is for our particular product. Therefore I say we should export manufactured goods also with our wheat and flour.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What are we going to get back for the wheat and flour and other merchandise that we export?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Does my hon. friend suggest that I am favouring a prohibitive tariff? I never mentioned a prohibitive tariff.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It has got to be, in order to build up industries. You say you want to build up home industries; you cannot build them up if you allow manufactured goods to come in.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Certainly, we cannot manufacture at the present time all the goods we import.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I see.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: But there are certain goods we should manufacture. I do not for a moment suggest that you should build a tariff fence so high that foreign goods cannot get over it-not at all. I have stated in clear and unmistakable language that all we ask is a cost-of-living tariff for the efficient manufacturer-for what we can manufacture here. In addition to that certain goods from England and other parts of the world will always enter under any tariff you may have, especially if it be only a reasonable cost-of-living tariff.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would the hon. member kindly specify some lines of goods that he would allow us to import?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is surely factious in putting to me such a question. He does not expect me to turn myself into a catalogue, does he?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, I do not really expect it.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am speaking in general terms, that is all. The general argument may be good or it may be bad, but it appeals to me, and I am putting it to my hon,. friends opposite as it appeals to me, simply as a reasonable argument-that no hasty, ill-advised changes be made in the tariff, but that any changes which may be proposed be carefully thought out, not confining ourselves to their probable effect on the immediate present, but looking into the future to see where such changes will land us. There is nothing unreasonable about that. I am not arguing for the East alone. It is ridiculous for the East to say to the West. "We are not interested in your welfare," just as ridiculous as it would be for the West to say to the East, "We will not have anything to do with your industries." We have to try to devise a fair and reasonable policy both for the East and for the West.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What is the East, may I ask my hon. friend? There are plenty of low-tariff men in the East as well as in the West.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am not drawing any particular line of demarcation. If my hon. friend so desires, I am willing to consider the Maritime provinces in with the West.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That affects your argument.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Let us put the Maritimes in with the West for the present. But it is
The Address-Mr. Marler
not a question on my part of talking about prohibition; it is a question of reason, of allowing our towns and cities to live, and unless we do this I claim that our agriculturists will be injured on account of their home market being seriously diminished. Surely, my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Hoey) will admit that if we had two million more people in the city of Montreal, they would consume at least two million more barrels of flour, which means in the neighborhood of ten million bushels of wheat.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
What will become of
the cities if the agricultural community is not allowed to live?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I expected, Mr. Speaker,
a barrage to come from that direction at this stage. I am not trying to put the agriculturist out of existence. I have endeavoured to suggest that there is much that can be done for the agriculturist; there are many taxes that can be taken off for his benefit, and I think that would be readily agreed to by every member of this House. But I submit that the tariff should not be such as to put the cities out of existence. I think we ought to have a reasonable cost of living tariff. Of course, if my hon. friends say, "No tariff," I have no desire and cannot submit an argument on that question. But what I claim is that the cities consume agricultural products and that unless the cities expand and grow, the home market will be lessened and the effects of that condition will be severely felt by the agricultural classes.
I was going to give the particulars with respect to a number of commodities, but I shall not take up the time of the House.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Go on.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Very well. I spoke about wheat a few moments ago; let me refer to one or two other commodities. In 1921 we produced over $74,000,000 worth of butter and cheese; our export of these products was $28,000,000 and our home consumption $55,000,000. In wool we produced in 1921 $2,975,000; we exported $242,000 and consumed at home $2,732,000. In 1923 we produced in eggs $48,770,000 worth; we exported this product to the value of $1,030,000 and the consumption at home was $47,740,000. In 1921 the value of our maple products was $4,318,000; our export was only $173,000 and we consumed at home $4,-
145,000.	In these few commodities alone, to say nothing of hosts of others, the value of the home consumption was $195,000,000, or $23 per head of the population. The exodus to the United States, of which I spoke a little while
The Address-Mr. Marler

ago, has meant a loss to agriculturists in this country in these products alone of over $7,500,000. Mr. Speaker,-and I say this with the greatest respect to any member of this House who disagrees with me-if the urban population increases our home market will increase with it and there will be a distinct advantage to the agriculturist, whereas if our population decreases there will be a very distinct disadvantage. The only way we can keep people in this country is to provide work for the rural dwellers as well as for the urban dwellers; to give all the population, no matter where we get it from, something to do.
I spoke a moment ago about the British preference, and perhaps some hon. members may have seen in what I said an indication that I thought the British preferential tariff might well not be kept in effect as it is at present. I do not disguise my feelings on that subject; at the same time I would be the last man in this House to hold the belief that we should not help Great Britain to the fullest extent of our ability. But I do not think we are helping Great Britain in this way. We are not helping Great Britain by making ourselves a weak nation; our great value to the Empire can only consist in our making ourselves a strong nation, in our taking upon ourselves our fair burdens for the Empire as they may come along. The only way to put ourselves in a position to do that is to build up our population. What we could do for Great Britain to-day would be to absorb many of her surplus population and give them work in our cities and towns, in our factories and so on. But we are not prepared to give them that to-day.
I think I have finished with most of the questions which might cause recrimination or questioning in this House. There are only two other matters that I should like to touch upon, and I shall not refer to them at great length. First is the question of stability in taxation. Undoubtedly we must have taxes. A tax is an impost for the benefit of government, and as such it must necessarily be for the benefit of the people on whom it is levied. In other words, if an impost is such as is difficult or impossible to collect, the very object of the tax will in time be defeated. We, in this country in the past-and I am not speaking of any particular government; I am referring to our genera! attitude with regard to taxation- have said that those who were successful should be taxed a little more, those who were more successful, still more, and that the most successful should be taxed the greatest amount. I am a believer in imposing taxes

where they can best be borne. There are certain industries in Canada at the present time, notably the agricultural industry, which cannot bear taxes as well as other industries can. There should be some alleviation, therefore, in that respect, and perhaps some other industry should have a tax imposed upon it in accordance with its means. Likewise the individual should be taxed according to his ability to pay. We have not taken the attitude, I think, that as partners in the state the people should be consulted before taxation is imposed, in order that the effect of the taxation may be understood and that the tax may be easily collected. As it stands now, taxation is getting more and more complicated; as a matter of fact we are rapidly turning ourselves into a nation of taxpayers and fillers in of forms. Why should we not consolidate our taxation so as to have it fall where it should rather than where it should not? Why should a government board of experts not be appointed to look into the whole question of taxation, to co-ordinate it, to have it thoroughly understood? Where it is seen that a certain business, a certain profession or certain individuals should get the benefit of an alleviation in the way of taxation, in order, perhaps, that they might be able to sell to others the products of their business, why should the tax not be taken off? In addition to that, under our present system the taxation laws emanate from one department of government and the collection of the tax is made by another. All these things, particularly at this perplexing period in our history, should be consolidated, simplified, made readily understandable, so arranged that business will be made easy and that every one can go ahead with the activities in which he is engaged without being under the necessity of continually thinking about taxes.
There is a great deal to be said in that connection. We have had experience in the matter of changes in the laws of taxation. Last year we made two very important changes, and I believe those changes were ill considered-not because we were not willing to consider them; not because the promoters were not acting in perfect good faith; not because the minister who introduced the bills was not acting in perfect good faith and did not desire to have the tax properly administered, but because we simpiy had not the time, or the ability, perhaps,- I say that subject to correction-to understand all the complicated matters involved, matters which could only be thoroughly understood after weeks of study.

The Address-Mr. Marler
Last year we made an amendment to the Special War Revenue Act-the sales tax. I say again that I do not for one moment attribute anything to the minister or to the promoters in that respect at all, but I venture to say that there were not six members of this House last year who understood that law, and I was not one of the six. The law as at present in force as regards the sales tax is a most complicated piece of legal machinery, difficult to administer, difficult to collect the tax, unfair in certain directions and open to grave misuses in others. As regards the unlicensed wholesaler it puts him in a most unfair position. As regards the unlicensed manufacturer, that is, the manufacturer not manufacturing up to $10,000, it is open to very, very grave abuse. I would ask the gov-vernment to take into consideration this matter of the sales tax again this year and to make such necessary amendments to it or so to revise our system of taxation that the people of this country having to bear the taxes may bear them as lightly as it is possible for them to do.
Another amendment we made last year was to our income tax law. That law as it stood, even without the amendment, was a law which had been made in times of stress. It was a perfectly proper law, a law that everybody should carry out to the letter, but I doubt very much whether it is carried out entirely to the letter in all respects. I doubt very much if everything that could be collected under that law is collected, but at the same time there are elements in the income tax law which put a great many qualities which we should have in this country, such as charity, ability, and energy, straight into the hands of mortmain. It puts millions and millions of dollars in mortmain every year, either because the tax is too heavy or because it is not properly applied. Much at the present time-I will not say is kept secretly hidden; those are not the words I intend to use at all-but much money is not put into circulation that should be put into circulation to help build up the country and expand it in every way because of our income tax law. Notwithstanding this lack of vision and this lack of heart as exemplified in our income tax law, what did we do last year? We brought down an amendment which created a prior lien on all the assets of the individual. I protested last year against this amendment. I told the government at that time, and I tell the government frankly again now, that if that amendment is persisted in, it will simply mean there will be no money to lend
on mortgage in this country. I feel quite confident also that when the banks fully grasp what that amendment means it will be very difficult to make loans of any kind, and very difficult to make conveyances of property. These matters are of vital importance to the West. Mortgage money must be loaned in the West. In the West there are at the present time serious restrictions on people lending money, but here the tax collector comes along, and, with the departmental mind entirely, not the mind of the people from whom the money is to be collected, but the departmental mind, says:	1
want a law put into effect that will make it as easy as possible for me to take the money away from the people, to stop your industry, to stop your commerce. Consequently that amendment was put on the statute books. I would solemnly warn the government that that amendment should certainly be repealed this year.
Mr. Speaker, I have spoken at very great length. I owe you and hon. members of this House my heartfelt thanks for the patience with which you have listened to me here to-day. I did not desire to speak at such length, but the matters which I have brought before the House to-day are of vital interest to the people I represent, and although I in no way presume to speak for them, I believe of vital interest to the whole city of Montreal.
In addition let me say this. Not only those in the constituency I here represent but every member from the province of Quebec, nay, every person in the province of Quebec, wishes to see preserved our British and French traditions to which we have been devoted from generation to generation. Many of us for many generations have known no other home outside of our province of Quebec. I do not speak for others, but I believe that those traditions can only be preserved by Canada, as Canada, going ahead and being kept for Canadians, and being a nation, as I stated at the beginning of my remarks, under the British Crown. That, sir, is the main object and the main theme that I have to lay before the House to-day and I beg hon. gentlemen to consider that; to consider the situation in which we place ourselves if our population declines, if our work people leave us, for in that case I feel confident that these traditions which we hold in the greatest reverence, which we learnt at our mother's knee and which we cherish so dearly, will also disappear and be lost to this country.

The Adress-Mr. MacKelvie
Mr. JOHN A. MacKELVIE (Yale): Mr. Speaker, before I address myself to a few points in connection with the Speech from the Throne' I would like with the same sincerity and heartiness which has characterized other speakers to compliment those who were responsible for moving and seconding the Address. I am sure they must have found it a rather difficult task this year, more so than in other sessions of the House I think, Mr. Speaker, for it must have been a somewhat agile mind, I might almost say a somewhat penetrating instinct, that could dig into the mass of tortuous verbiage which comprised the Speech of this year, and bring out any fruitful theme for congratulation so far as the government of this country is concerned.
I do not intend to follow the remarks of the previous speaker (Mr. Marler) for the" simple reason that the latter part of his address was one with which I find myself most thoroughly in sympathy. Indeed, it is one which anyone in this group in the House might be proud to see on record with his own name above it. So far as the last part of his address was concerned, it so directly and pointedly featured the speech which the right hon. leader of this party recently made in Montreal that one could not fail to be impressed with the fact that that speech had sunk very deeply into the consciousness of the speaker, and in his estimation it required very serious rebuttal indeed. I will leave it to the House and to the intelligence of the country to give a verdict as to whether that rebuttal was as effective as the speaker no doubt intended it to be.
Mr. Speaker, I said that the Speech from the Throne was one in which it was difficult to find matters upon which the government could be very distinctly congratulated. Before I make reference to certain points contained therein I would like to mention a fact that must be of particular interest to this House, and that is that to-day the members received in their post office boxes a copy of the report of the proceedings of the Imperial Conference. I have not yet had the opportunity to read that report and to give it the. attention I have no doubt it deserves. I expect to find it very interesting reading, but I need not hope to find within its covers any statement that will show to the people of Canada that the Canadian representatives at that conference gave the support to Mr. Baldwin's proposals that the people of this country expected they would at that time. Mr. Baldwin laid before the country his proposals. When the attention of our people was

directed towards his scheme of fiscal reform in the Old Country, his policy of preferential tariffs within the Empire, it was rather humiliating, to say the least, to those who hold the opinions that are held by this group in the House-in fact I think by a good many sections of our population-it was more than humiliating, it was intensely aggravating to know that the policy which we so ardently desired to see pressed forward was supported by the Prime Ministers of South Africa, Australia and New Zealand, and that our own representative not onljv sat silent at the conference where the policy was propounded but in any expression that he gave to his sentiments-which assuredly were not the sentiments of Canada-intimated that all these matters were of no concern. So evidently was that position made clear by the Canadian representative that Mr. Asquith, during the recent .election campaign in Great Britain, was enabled to deliver a speech in which he said that the matter of preferential tariffs was not one in which the dominions were very greatly interested, or one upon which they based any demand. In making this statement Mr. Asquith could only have had in mind the Dominion of Canada-surely the greatest of all the dominions-and he even went so far as to say practically that it was not the desire of Canada that any such policy should be brought into effect.
Now, Mr. Speaker, coming as I do from a province which was vitally interested in that fiscal policy, coming as I do from a constituency which more than any other is intensely interested in it, I feel that some attention should be directed in this House to the course taken by the Prime Minister of Canada in so representing-I think I am justified in saying, in so misrepresenting,-this Dominion on that occasion. The value of such preferential treatment on the part of Great Britain to our constituency of Yale would be such that I could hardly describe it in words. The prime interest of the constituency, as a great many members here are aware, has to do with the fruit growing industry, and a preference such as was contemplated of five shillings per hundred pounds on imported fruit would have placed our fruit growers in such a position that they would once more have seen a ray of hope ahead, whereas to-day they are almost as much disappointed as the wheat growers of the prairies are if we are to believe the stories told by our Progressive friends.
In regard to this question of tariff preference Mr. Baldwin had the courage of his convictions. He went to the country but unfortunately did not return to parliament

The Address-Mr. MacKelvie
with a majority. Nevertheless Mr. Baldwin sowed seed which will yet bear fruit, he delivered a message which future generations will read and which perhaps will come into effect even in our own time. By those of us who believe in the great and beneficent influence which the British Empire is destined to exercise in the world the happiest results were anticipated from Mr. Baldwin's plan. His vision was such that when he surveyed the whole field he realized what would follow from close inter-relationship between the different parts of the Empire; he saw the Empire drawn together by bonds of mutual interest and strengthened by a preferential tariff which would give it a place in the world such as perhaps none of us have ever dreamed to be possible. But the policy of negation, the policy of discouragement, advanced by our representative at that conference, will perhaps set the wheels of progress back for several years.
I do not know just exactly how His Excellency was made to give the expression in the Speech from the Throne that Canada is now such an extremely prosperous country.
I have found that this statement received little support in any of the speeches so far delivered here. Our Progressive friends, through the mouthpiece of their leader, have assured us that the agricultural part of the community is anything but prosperous. That hon. gentleman went further and related that only one-third of the number of agricultural implements were sold now that were sold fifteen years ago, which is a pretty clear indication, that the manufacturing industry is not revelling in prosperity. The speaker who immediately preceded me also laid facts before the House which force one to reach the same conclusion. Speaking for my own consituency I have no doubt in the world that conditions there will have to be vastly improved from what they are to-day before we can claim anything approaching a measure of prosperity and happiness. For the existing evil there is a remedy, a remedy which I hope to advance during the course of my remarks but I see no indication of that remedy being applied by the present administration. Indeed I am firmly convinced that instead of bringing about a [DOT] better condition of affairs the policy forecasted in the Speech from the Throne will be very certain to make existing conditions much worse. The remedy which I would desire to apply to the financial depression in Canada rests entirely in a properly devised and vigorously constructed tariff of protection. It is no news to the members of this House that I am a thorough going protectionist. It is one of the
political principles to which I am most firmly anchored; and I like to congratulate myself that I belong to a party which through storm and stress, whether in power or out of power, has never deviated from the policy devised by our great leader, Sir John Macdonald, when he lifted this country out of the slough of depression and set it upon the high road to prosperity and when he unfurled the standard of a protective tariff. That standard has always waved and has never been lowered. Our present leader holds it aloft and has done so in his campaign from coast to coast. In all circumstances and in all places he has firmly adhered to the principles of his party, and has never deviated from them. In that fact we rejoice as a party. To that policy we point the people of this country as likely to yield them relief from the present depressing conditions.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Before the House adjourned at 6 o'clock I had been making some observations regarding the Speech from the Throne, and had said, among other things, that so far from being able to endorse the statements put into the mouth of His Excellency regarding the prosperous condition of Canada as a whole, I felt, greatly against my desire as a Canadian, to doubt if these things were true, and I felt compelled to take exception to that statement. I gave as an example the depressed condition of my own community and the hard struggle which fruitgrowing sections of British Columbia were having to make ends meet, and, this, Sir, despite the fact that no part of Canada possesses land so admirably suited to the production of fruit and vegetables as the section which I have the honour to represent. Nature indeed seems to have intended it as a district in which the cultivation of fruit and vegetables could be most successfully prosecuted, and yet, owing to this very depression of which I am speaking, the fruit-growers of that country this year have found themselves unable to profitably market what was indeed a very large and good crop. I said that among the remedies which might be applied to cure, or at least to ameliorate, this condition was the old remedy of adequate protection which had so successfully brought this country at another period of its existence out of a condition of stagnation and depression into one of prosperity and progress.



The Address-Mr. MacKelvie
Tariff, Mr. Speaker, has been the weapon for generations in this country in the hands of statesmen, which they have utilized not only to build up progress in the industrial, commercial and agricultural communities of the land, but at times it has been in their hands a weapon with which to negotiate for better terms in other countries. It is absurd in my opinion to term the present existing tariff of Canada as anything approaching a real protective tariff. When every country in the world which has a tariff has been building up its barriers against this country for years, when we are shut out practically from the markets of the republic to the south, which has prospered as everybody knows to a wonderful degree under that same system of protection, when, as we look abroad we find no indication of any country in the world seeking to lower its duties, I say that it is nothing short of an absurdity to term the tariff which now obtains in this country one of adequate protection. If I had my way particular attention would be given to the revision of the tariff, to bring it to a condition that would give real protection, not only to the industries of the country, but more particularly to the farming community.
I am firmly convinced that the interests of the farming community would be greatly benefited, that the country would become enriched and that prosperity would follow in its train, if the products of the soil were given a protection at least equal to twice that which now obtains. I would have our butter, eggs and vegetables and all the products of the soil subject to a customs tariff which would in some measure prevent competition from the south. I wonder with what degree of confidence those of my hon. friends in the Progressive group who place, or appear to place, their faith in a policy of reciprocity with the United States, could, under existing conditions, approach that country and attempt to negotiate with them. The United States would simply laugh at them. They would say "We give everything and receive practically nothing in return". Of course I am no believer in reciprocity with the United States. I believe that nothing would tend to bring about in a shorter time, the ruin of Canada, the ruin of our industrial concerns and our agriculturists, and, in part, the ruin of our railways than any arrangement of that kind with our neighbours to the south. But even if we desired to negotiate such an arrangement, it would be ridiculous to approach them with any such bargain as we are able to offer at present.
The fruit-growers of my district, who are believers in protection as I have indicated, see

more than one way of getting protection for their industry. One of these is by a tariff, but not like our present tariff. The other is by a dumping clause, which gives them protection from the stuff dumped from the south of the line, where it has been raised and produced much earlier than in our own country. A resolution has been placed in my hands by the Associated Boards of Trade of British Columbia. Those boards of trade are not more particularly interested in the fruit-growing industry than in any other business interests of the province, but knowing, as they do, that some forty million dollars is invested in the fruit industry, and that it is suffering from very serious handicaps at present; they realize that the old dumping clause which was brought in by the previous government was a clause with teeth in it, which gripped and functioned. I wish the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) were here to listen to what I am saying. I pause here to pay a tribute to the manner in which he has administered the existing act. The principle that protection should be given by order in council and that it should be left entirely to the discretion of the Minister of Customs is nothing more than vicious. I would say to the hon. minister who has charge of that department that he has endeavoured, I think, properly, to put the dumping clause into execution, and has instructed his officials to see that it was operated in the best possible manner. As I said before, it depends entirely upon who occupies that position. We may have a Minister of Customs at any time who would do little or nothing to meet the requirements of our fruit-growing population, as he might not be sympathetic towards them and might be a believer in free trade in all matters; and under his regime nothing but disaster would come to the fruit-growing industry. So, therefore, realizing the position of this industry, the Associated Boards of Trade of British Columbia have placed in my hands the following resolution-
Whereas general prosperity must be built upon profitable agriculture, which can only be realized if farmers are enabled to sell their products at reasonable profits ; and
Whereas it is detrimental to the best interests of all classes of the community that products of the soil bo sold at less than their cost of production to the grower in Canada; and
Whereas products of the soil are frequently offered from foreign countries at prices which are considerably less than cost of production;
Be it therefore resolved;-That the hon. the Minister of Customs, be urged to apply the dumping penalty to all importations of agricultural products sold at less than Canadian cost of production, bearing in mind the following points;-
1. The Department of Customs be asked to publish cost of production figures for all agricultural products produced in Canada, not later than June 1st in each

The Address-Mr. MacKelvie
year, such list to be in effect for one year, and that it be provided that when Canadian products are available and importations are invoiced at less than cost of production, a special dumping duty be collected, equal to the difference between the fair market value as established by the above-mentioned list, and the price at which such fruit was imported.
2. Dumping penalty should only be applied to importations made at such times as similar products are available in Canada.
After considering this very vexed problem very carefully, this is the conclusion which the Associated Boards of Trade in my province have reached in the matter. They are not advocates of the fruit-growing industry in particular; they are interested in the general prosperity of the province; and in view of the fact that such an immense amount of capital is invested in this important industry they have come to the conclusion that the present dumping clause needs to be amended in this direction. I am cordially in sympathy with the resolution. I do not say that, perhaps, it might not be improved upon. I believe, from the experience we have had during the last few years, that even the excellent dumping clause which was put into operation by the previous government could be improved in some important respects. I have tried to put the matter before the House as briefly as possible. A large percentage of the fruit growers are to-day suffering from this depression throughout Canada and it is impossible for them in the present state of affairs to find profitable markets.
Now, I am not going to argue the pros and cons of a protective policy; the matter was admirably treated this afternoon by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler). In my opinion, many vexatious problems which face the people to-day would be much more easy of solution were an adequate policy of protection such as I have indicated put into force. I believe it would have a wonderful effect on immigration; it would also tend to prevent emigration. If we can build up towns and cities in this country by establishing prosperous industrial concerns, thus providing employment for large numbers of workmen, we shall have no difficulty in retaining those of our population who are now seeking employment in the country to the south of us which has been made prosperous by virtue of a protective policy. Far from there being a steady stream of emigration from this country, we should be able to retain our population and attract back to the country many of our people who have left. But in my opinion this can be done only by having a reasonable policy of protection.
8J
I was not able this afternoon to follow the line of argument advanced by my hon. friend from Montreal. I did understand, however, that he was endeavouring to refute some of the figures submitted to this House in his speech by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen). But be the figures as they may, the personal observations of practically every member of this House must have led him to the conclusion that emigration from this country is a very serious matter at the present moment. I know of no section where the people will not tell you that they have lost hundreds, and indeed thousands, of their best citizens within the last few years. To stem this exodus is a matter that calls for the best attention of any government. What remedy is suggested by the present administration? I have heard nothing so far indicated in the speech of any hon. member, nor is there anything in the Speech from the Throne to show that the government has any really effective remedy in view.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I shall come to that
presently; that certainly will have a marked effect in certain parts of the country. After all, we might dilate on this question of protection at very great length, but so far as I can recollect no one has summed up the matter in more concise terms than was done on one occasion by one of the greatest statesmen and patriots which this continent has ever produced. Abraham Lincoln said that if a man buys goods abroad he has the goods while the other country has the money, whereas if he buys those goods at home he has the goods and his own country has the money also. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) interjected a moment ago a remark the purport of which was that among the means of preventing emigration and of encouraging people to come to the country would be the branch lines policy of the government. I was glad to note that paragraph in the Speech from the Throne which referred to the continued prosperity of the National Railways. The figures which nave been given to the country by the president of those railways during the past few months have been indeed encouraging to the people. While perhaps the president has built upon the splendid foundation laid by his predecessor, apparently he, or someone at least, has been responsible for a very marked improvement in one direction in the service of the National Railways: I refer to the esprit de corps which seems now to obtain among all the officials from the highest to the lowest. It is now a pleasure

The Address-Mr. MacKelvie
to meet them; they seem to be imbued with the idea that the service demands their hearty attention and support, and evidently they are out to give that attention and support. That no doubt is responsible in no small measure for the increased business in connection with the National lines.
Coming now to the question [DOT] raised by the Minister of Railways, I wish to refer to the matter that really urged me in getting to my feet. For several years I have been working as hard as possible in this parliament to bring about the completion of a branch line running through my constituency from Kamloops to Kelowna on the Canadian National line. It has been graded for several years and the country has expended $5,250,000 upon it. The arguments for the completion of this branch line are perhaps as strong, as forcible and as unanswerable as those that can be advanced for any similar branch line in the Dominion. I have submitted them to the House at previous sessions, and I consider it my duty on this occasion again to call the attention of the government and of parliament to the matter. In the first place, we have already, as I say, expended on that branch line over $5,000,000. It is lying idle and so long as it does so we shall lose the interest on that money which, at 6 per cent, would represent over $300,000 a year. Naturally the line is deteriorating every year, and it is only a question of time when the grade will be of no further service and will have to be reconstructed if the line is completed. This branch line will serve a wonderfully productive country and will open up a new district. Passing from Kamloops through Grand Prairie and the Falkland districts, it will open up a country untouched by any transportation system. In Falkland there is, I think, the largest pure deposit of gypsum on the continent, owned by a Winnipeg firm who are only too anxious to exploit it as soon as there are the necessary transportation facilities. A sixteen mile spur from my town of Vernon to Lumby passes through a rich and thickly settled agricultural and horticultural district. It goes through the famous Coldstream ranch, and when it reaches Lumby it enters a district of wonderful fertility, a mixed farming district that produces grain and hay, and from which are exported considerable wood products such as telephone and telegraph poles, railway ties and so forth. This would bring a steady stream of revenue to the main line. From Vernon to Kelowna you have a district containing 60 per cent, of the fruit growing population of

the Okanagan, and it is estimated that these men in this 35 miles are losing $200,000 a year at the present time in transportation charges, trucking their fruit to points upon the Canadian Pacific railway which would be touched by this new line. This would give them cheaper transportation facilities, and as I have already pointed out we are paying $300,000 in interest charges while our farmers are losing much money to-day trucking their products, and it would surely be a matter of economy to complete this branch line. Out of that valley this year went over ten thousand cars of fruit and vegetables and other products, and there was of course considerable incoming freight. It is estimated that the local revenue to the railway is upwards of three million dollars a year, and a very large share of that revenue would go to the National lines were this branch completed. I think I am giving a very conservative figure indeed when I say that the first year after its completion the National lines would receive at least a million dollars of traffic.
Now, as I have said, I have been exerting what abilities I possess in trying for some years to bring this matter before parliament and get the line completed. Hon. members can easily understand with what a feeling of despair I went home last year. True, the bill passed this House, but it was framed in such a way that the Senate immediately took exception to it and killed it the last day of the session. I was surprised to hear the right hon. Prime Minister say to the leader of the opposition the other night:	"Your friends
in the Senate killed that bill." The right hon. gentleman must have been extremely ill informed, or else he was endeavouring to deliberately deceive the House. It was not in particular the friends of the right hon. leader of the opposition in the Senate who killed that bill, for only ten votes could be scratched up in its favour, so it is not very difficult to understand that the feeling against the bill was by no means confined to the Conservative element in the upper house. Indeed, the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), I apprehend, is perfectly cognizant of the opposition in the Senate; it came from every quarter.
Greatly to my disappointment I have recently been informed-I do not know how good my authority is-that it is the intention of the government to again introduce a bill along somewhat similar lines to the ill-fated measure of last session. This, to me, would indicate that they are absolutely courting defeat, and it gives rise to the impression, which I have heard expressed in more than one

The Address-Mr. MacKelvie
section of the Dominion, that the government are not sincere in their intentions and for some reason or other, which I cannot fathom, would like to have the bill killed again. I know Sir Henry Thornton recognizes the importance of this branch line in that it would be one of the best feeders to the National system, but I do not know, and I have never been able to find anybody who could inform me, why it is that this year there is a chance of the government again introducing the bill in the same shape as they brought it down last session, which means that the Senate will mete out to it the same treatment.
I would implore the Minister of Railways to deal with these branch lines in separate bills this session, and so let each stand on its own merits. For the reasons which I have advanced to-night, and which I could enlarge upon if necessary, I have no doubt that the Senate can be persuaded that the Kam-loops-Kelowna branch line is absolutely justified; and I am equally confident that the Senate will look with favour on similar branch lines on the prairies which have been graded for years and which would serve a country urgently in need of transportation for its grain, which at present has to be hauled long distances to the nearest railway.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Does my hon. friend intimate that the Senate has not any power to amend a bill of this kind?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No, I do not exactly
intimate that, Mr. Speaker; but I doubt the wisdom of cumbering such a bill with all sorts of what the Senate seem to conceive to be impossible conditions, when each line might well be the subject of a separate estimate, thus standing upon its own merits. I can conceive no possible objection to this course. The hon. minister has intimated that it would be difficult to keep the money flowing to cover the construction work on these lines after it is once started, but that has never been an insuperable difficulty in connection with any other public undertaking, and I do not see why it could not be overcome in this connection.

friends surrounding me and those in the Progressive party who are interested in these branch lines present a united front in renewing their request to the minister to bring down this branch line legislation in such shape that- there will be no danger of its meeting the same fate again in the upper house.

speechtext: Does my hon. friend think that is the real reason the Senate threw out the bill last session?

speechtext:
That is the reason given.
I acknowledge that possibly there were some other influences at work which I cannot control; but there was the situation as it appeared before the public. The Senate gave their reasons for throwing out the bill, and in a general way the public regarded those reasons as pretty good.	.

speechtext: That is not my information.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am not upholding the Senate; indeed the hon. minister will understand that it was a very severe blow to me when the measure was defeated in the upper house. At the same time, if he will read the Senate debates of yesterday he will observe that hon. Senator Turriff intimated in very plain language that the bill as presented to the Senate was very obnoxious. I do not suppose I can say anything further to convince the minister if he is not already convinced, but I do hope that those of us who are interested in these branch lines will not have to go home to our constituents at the end of this session with the same sorry tale as we had to tell them last year. If unhappily we have to, nothing will convince those constituents that the government did not deliberately court defeat of the bill in the Senate, knowing exactly what reception it would receive there.
Something was said this afternoon by the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Marler) regarding the taxation problems which confront this country. None of us who have given any study to the situation at all have failed to reach the conclusion that industry to-day is stifled by excess taxation. The problem of how to ameliorate that condition lies in the hands of the government, and so far the only indication they have given of any remedial policy is that they intend to make a reduction in the tariff on the instruments of production-a policy which, as I have tried to point out before, instead of being a remedy would aggravate an already desperate situation.
The hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Marler) also had something to say respecting the sales tax. I do not know whether it is possible to abolish that tax, but I do believe it could be readjusted to lighten its incidence. An extremely inequitable provision is that which exempts firms doing less than ten thousand dollars of business a year. I know

The Address-Mr. MacKelvie
a firm in my own constituency employing ten oy twelve men, with over a ten thousand dollar turnover, and I also know a rival firm in which the two principals do their own work and come under the exemption clause. The night before I left for Ottawa I visited a moving picture theatre and saw flashed on the screen: Buy your products from So-and-So and save the 6 per cent sales tax. There is a most glaring instance of unequal apportionment of taxation, and surely it is something which the government, if it believes in a policy of fair dealing, will take haste to remedy before this session closes.
To-day a gentleman brought to my attention a matter on which I had not intended to speak, but which I know has been very fully pressed upon the attention of the government for some time back, and that is the condition of depositors of the Home Bank who have suffered such severe losses. Fortunately for me and my community there were no branches of this bank in my constituency. This gentleman comes from the mining town of Fernie, in East Kootenay, and the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) will no doubt agree that what he said was absolutely correct. He told of a most deplorable condition in that community, miners, many of them old men who had reached the end of their working days and whose entire savings had been deposited in that bank, were left absolutely penniless. I have no remedy to suggest; it is not my duty to do so at this juncture, but I do think that the proposals of the government to sidestep the issue and to start on its jauntings another commission to make an inquiry in a restricted way into what happened in connection with this bank during a certain period is like passing out a stone to those people who are demanding bread. The right hon. leader of the House intimated yesterday when pressure was brought to bear upon him, that he would extend the scope of this commission, but the result is problematical, to say the least, no matter how far its scope is extended. In any case I think it is only right, as suggested by the right hon. leader of the opposition, that the inquiry should go right back to the time of the issuing of the charter and take in those years when Hon. A. K. Maclean was handling the finances of this country as well as the time when Sir Thomas White was Minister of Finance in the Union government. The connection with it of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is also one which he would gladly see probed. But this solution suggested to the broken-hearted and impoverished depositors of the Home Bank

throughout Canada will bring them very little relief indeed.
I spoke briefly this afternoon of the effects of the Imperial Conference in London, one of which was to force to the country the then government headed by Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin. I should not have said " force "; he went to the country because he thought it the right thing to do. Mr. Baldwin said that his predecessor in office had made a pledge during the election campaign as a result of which he was elected that during his regime there would be no interference with the fiscal policy of Great Britain. Mr. Baldwin could, if he so desired, force through his preferential tariff policies, he had a sufficient majority to carry them into effect; but he considered himself in honour bound to refer the matter to the electorate.
I can draw something approaching a parallel in this connection:	Last session this House was
informed by the government through the hon. Minister of Finance that the present tariff had at last reached the condition where it could be termed a stabilized tariff. That promise went out from the government through the Minister of Finance to the country, and I have no doubt that business men in all parts of Canada governed themselves accordingly and made their arrangements, firmly believing the pledge that had been given and that there would be no interference during the remainder of the present term of parliament. If they are to be disappointed; if this solemn pledge from the government is to be violated, is the government in a very different position from that of Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin when he conceived it his bounden duty to make an appeal to the electorate of Great Britain? Those of us who were in this House during the session of 1921 heard from the then opposition, the present party in office-from the present Prime Minister and many of his followers-insistent and vociferous demands that the administration of that day should make an immediate appeal to the country. They said, "You have no mandate from the people; the people have lost confidence in you; it is your duty to go to the country.'' And there seemed to be a certain amount of justice in their contention; the government of the day had carried on for a considerable length of time. At any rate, the result was an appeal to the country. I am free to state, if my judgment is worth anything in political matters, that I have discovered in traversing this country from east to west and from west to east a feeling which indicates very clearly that the people of Canada to-day have entirely lost confidence in this government.

The Address-Mr. Stork
The right hon. Prime Minister the other night, replying to the leader of the opposition, sought to pooh-pooh the significance of the by-elections in Halifax and Kent. He said, "Oh, after all, these elections were determined upon purely local issues. They do not affect the position of the government in the slightest. Such things happen; by-elections of this kind have at present no particular political significance." Well, I venture to say that if the government will do as they should do; if they will decide that having broken or being about to break the pledge given so emphatically and so explicitly at the last session of this parliament by the Finance Minister; if they will take the honourable course as did the Hon. Mr. Baldwin and make an immediate appeal to the country, they will find, I am firmly convinced, that there was far more significance in the by-elections in Halifax and Kent than the Prime Minister wishes to convey to this House.
