speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the brief remarks which I desire to make to the House to-night, I hope I shall not be regarded as speaking in a parochial or provincial way, but in view of the present necessities of the district of Skeena, and in view also of the enormous size of that constituency, I believe that in taking on any more territory I should be transgressing the rules of good taste. Therefore I desire to-night to address my remarks particularly to the central portion of British Columbia, from which I come.
At the outset let me offer my congratulations to the government on the Speech from the Throne, in that it indicates a reduction of taxation and also a general improvement of the conditions generally throughout the Dominion of Canada. More particularly do I wish to congratulate the government on its attention to the fishing industry of British Columbia. During the session of 1922, in accordance with a resolution passed by the Fisheries Committee of this House, the government appointed a royal commission to investigate the conditions of the fishing industry on the Pacific coast. By reason of my having been honoured with a seat on that commission I am perhaps precluded from being fulsome in my praises, but permit me to say without any flattery that the work of that commission was good and that it was highly appreciated by the people of British Columbia. There have been many commissions of a similar nature touring the province, and I am free to confess that the impression thej' left with the people was not of the best. When our commission came along in 1922 the
people in the West were wont to remark that this was just another of those joy riding affairs from which very little in the way of results could be expected. But the commission known as the Duff Commission carried out a most thorough investigation and it brought down a report upon which, I am glad to say, the government took immediate action.
One of the great issues in the province was the employment in the fisheries of nationalities other than the whites or Indians. That was a very burning question with the people who live on the Pacific coast. The recommendation of the commission was that in their estimation those other than whites or Indians should be reduced by forty per cent. Much opposition was offered to the suggestion that that reduction would not interfere with the proper operation of the fishing industry. Anyway, the suggestion was carried into effect, and I am glad to report to you, Sir, that all the people resident along the Pacific coast are of the opinion that that was a very wise measure and that it has worked no injury to the industry. I have in my possession several letters from those engaged in the canning business, and they claim it is a good measure and imposes no handicap on them. We were fortunate last year in that we had a bumper harvest of salmon in the salmon rivers of the Pacific coast. We look to a further good season this year and we hope from time to time to see the white citizens of this country given ample opportunity to develop the fisheries of that province.
Another improvement we are very glad to observe in connection with the progress of our fisheries, and that is that while on the Fraser river for a number of years back they have been allowed to use the fishing method known as the " gas boat," for some reason or other those who fish for a living on the Skeena and the Naas rivers in the north have been compelled to use the old British Columbia fishing boat equipped with a sail and oar. I never could appreciate why such a distinction should be made, but this commission that was out there last year, known as the Duff Commission, recommended that commencing with the year 1924 the use of gas boats be permitted on the Skeena. That recommendation comes into effect this year, and I know and am sure that the people who are making a living fishing will find it a very great advantage. I think if anything the regulations should have been just the reverse. The waters of the Fraser would be much more suitable for a boat with sail and oar than the placid waters of the Skeena.
The Address-Mr. Stork

But we are to have the gas boat this year and it will be a great advantage to the people who make their living from the waters of the north.
Another improvement inaugurated last year was a hydroplane patrol of waters of the north. It is a great task and very expensive, and last year the department inaugurated the plan of having a hydroplane for doing that work, and it is proving most efficient. We look forward this year to an increase in that service, because I am sure the department will find that as well as being efficient it is also very economical.
There is another aspect of the fisheries in regard to British Columbia that I wish to mention, and that is the progress of the halibut trade. The construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific to the northern port has completely revolutionized the halibut fishing industry. The railroad is now built to the fishing banks. Heretofore that trade was centered in the cities of Seattle and Vancouver, but it has followed the railways up north and to-day is centered in Prince Rupert. In 1923 twenty-nine and a half million pounds of halibut were marketed over the docks of the port of Prince Rupert. To convey that product to market required some fifteen hundred refrigerator cars, each car bringing a revenue to the Canadian National Railways of between $800 and $1,000. This development of the halibut fisheries has been one of the outstanding features of northern development, but the centralization of the trade also brings with it fresh problems and difficulties. Our Canadian fishermen who operate in that port are handicapped by the imposition of two cents a pound American duty. That is a burning question with the Canadian fishermen of the north, and they have protested repeatedly to the government here asking them to take whatever steps can be taken to have the duty removed. The Boat Owners' Association of that town have requested the government, in order to force this duty off, to close the port to American fisheries, but other interests in that port do not wish to see that drastic step taken. No one, I am sure, desires that the port be closed. What they do desire is that the duty be removed, and I as their representative would urge upon the government the necessity of continuing negotiations at Washington with a view to having this duty removed, because it is a grievous handicap and a great source of irritation and friction to the Canadian fishermen.
The waters of the Canadian Pacific fishing grounds are divided into three sections for

the purposes of departmental administration. They are known as sections or districts Nos. 1, 2 and 3. No. 1 has its headquarters in the city of New Westminster; No. 2 has its headquarters in the city of Prince Rupert, and No. 3 has its headquarters in the city of Nanaimo. For a long time the fisheries were administered through these separate and distinct headquarters. Then a system of centralization grew up, and of late years a central office has been opened in the city of Vancouver. This does not in my estimation make for economy or efficiency. We have in the central office in Vancouver a considerable overhead expense. We have there a considerable staff, and all the positions are under the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. Eight of these officials do considerable travelling from time to time, and I am thoroughly satisfied that with the salaries indicated here, plus the travelling expenses, plus also the office rental and upkeep, the total cost to the country will be in the neighbourhood of $50,000. When I first came to Ottawa two years ago I took this matter up with the department. I took it up last session, and I am taking it up again this session. I took this matter up before there was any mention of " A whisper of death " or " A carnival of extravagance." So in pressing it upon the government I trust I am not stealing anyone's copyright in this connection. I would suggest that the office be abolished immediately. I am satisfied that to revert to the old style method of having each district report directly as an independent unit to headquarters at Ottawa will make in greater degree for efficiency and for economy. Take for instance a patrolman, or a fish guardian as we call them, on the Naas river who is in doubt in regard to the operation of the

regulations. He has to communicate with the inspector at Prince Rupert. The inspector at Prince Rupert writes to the chief inspector at Vancouver, who in turn gets in touch with headquarters at Ottawa. Ottawa addresses its reply to the chief inspector at Vancouver, the latter sends the message on to the inspector at Prince Rupert, who in turn com- ' municates with the official on the Naas river. By that time the fish has escaped from the net, or some fellow over in Alaska has got away with it. I am fully satisfied that no reasons based on good economy justify the maintenance of this office. New Westminister has a district office twelve miles removed from the central office. In Nanaimo there is another district office forty miles away from the head office. My advice to the minister would be to close these offices at once and save the country some $50,000 a year, and then to give $1,000 each to the three districts in order to improve conditions there. The chief inspector in the city of Prince Rupert starts work in that position at a salary of $140 a month. In view of his responsibilities, in view of the tremendous amount of work he has to do, $140 a month is a very inadequate remuneration. Before an official can qualify for a position of that kind he has to serve in the department, and in view of this system of promotion he is an old man long before he can attain the position of inspector of the district where he will receive the princely salary of $140 a month. He can start in at a- minimum salary of $1,680 per annum and the maximum to which he can attain is $2,280 per annum. I think the schedule should be reversed, and that when the official reaches this office after long years of patient work he should receive the maximum of $2,280 and that thereafter the salary should be graded down to $1,680. Because by the time the official has served for five years in this capacity, after many years of faithful service in the department, he is a subject for the old men's home. Where you have a man, such as -we have at the present time, in charge of the district office in district No. 2, and where he commences at $140 a month, I consider such a salary is not in the interest of true economy. I would suggest, as I have already stated, that $1,000 of the money saved in the manner indicated be appropriated to the three fishery districts, and distributed in such a way as to improve the working conditions of the men who work in the fishery offices.
Now, Mr. Speaker, one of the outstanding features of western development has been the wonderful growth of the grain trade going
The Address-Mr. Stork
to the Pacific ocean. The Rocky mountains form a great barrier between the prairies of the West and the Pacific ocean, but this mountain range is cut by two passes, the Kicking Horse pass and the Yellowhead pass.
A few years ago only a small trickle of grain found its way through the mountain passes down to the waters of the Pacific. This small rivulet has grown to a torrent in the last couple of years, and last year it assumed the proportions of a mighty and swelling river. This growth will continue as the years go on. The grain movement to the Pacific coast has come to stay, and to-night I beseech this government to construct in the port of Prince Rupert a grain elevator so that some of this trade may be diverted to that port, and so that the Canadian National Railways may derive some benefit from the traffic which will flow over the tracks of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The city of Edmonton is the natural grain centre for central and northern Alberta, and for a large portion of the province of Saskatchewan. The government is building an elevator today in that city. That elevator in Edmonton will not fulfil its proper functions unless there is also an elevator in the port of Prince Rupert to which its wheat cargoes can be transmitted.
I desire to associate myself, with all the power and energy I possess, with deputations and delegations from that country to Ottawa, with resolutions of the Prince Rupert Board of. Trade backed by the resolutions from the Board of Trade of Edmonton, with newspaper editorials from the press of both sides of politics, and with letters and telegrams innumerable urging the construction of a grain elevator in the port of Prince Rupert. The Grand Trunk Pacific railway was the product of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government. That great statesman intended the completed Grand Trunk Pacific to be a monument to his memory in the same way that the construction of the Canadian Pacific stands to the credit of the late Sir John A. Macdonald. About 1905 or 1906 the government of Sir Wilfrid projected the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific. They said they were going to open and develop a new and wonderful country. The idea caught on throughout the whole of the Dominion; and people became convinced that the railway was a sound project and that it would open up a country that was well worth developing. The settlers who have gone into that northern country have proved to the satisfaction of the country, and to the satisfaction of those who initiated this railway in the first place, that the project was a sound one. There is tributary to
The Address-Mr. Stork

tile Grand Trunk Pacific 3,200,000 acres of agricultural land. The Mackenzie and Peace river country, which is an empire in itself, will pour its products out to the Pacific over the lines of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. That country to-day is peopled with settlers who have suffered intensely for lack of adequate railway facilities. The Grand Trunk Pacific runs through the Skeena country for a distance of 350 miles. It serves the Nechaco valley, the Bulkley valley, the -Skeena valley, the Kispiox valley, the Kitsumkalum valley, and Lakelse valley, each an empire in itself. These valleys are filled with settlers who are carrying on agricultural development as beat they can. They are not meeting
9	p. m. with very much success because local freight rates to the market are so high they can only with great difficulty make a living.
Local freight rates are based entirely upon transportation costs, and there is no immediate outlook for relief in the matter of local freight rate reduction, when w,e consider that we only have two or three freight trains a week travelling over the line when there should be four or five; and therefore these settlers to a man are demanding that traffic over the road be increased by the handling of wheat, so that the volume of trade over that road will make that particular branch pay. In that way they have some hope of relief and redress in the matter of local rates. Our terminal rates are the same from Edmonton to Prince Rupert as they are from Edmonton to Vancouver. This 350 miles of railroad running through the district of Skeena is manned by a great number of railway employees. We have firemen, engineers, conductors and breakmen, and all of the staff required to operate a railway. These men are only working a short time, because railway men are paid by the mile, and not by the day or the week. These men have been hanging on for years, expecting the fulfilment of the Laurier programme and the development of the Grand Trunk Pacific. They have been waiting and hoping for the development to take place; so have the settlers along that line.
But I can say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the people have no intention of remaining in their present condition indefinitely. They desire and they demand to be told what the policy of this government is towards the Grand Trunk Pacific. If these people are given to understand that there is to be no further development in the port of Prince Rupert they will govern their conduct accordingly. They will be able to map out their course for the

future, but they do insist upon finding out at the earliest possible moment what the intention of the government may be towards the completion of the Laurier idea. The greatest argument I have in connection with pressing the claim for the construction of this elevator is that it will bring traffic to the Canadian National Railways. It will furnish for the farmers the cheapest market and the cheapest outlet available on the Pacific coast. They will find that at the port of Prince Rupert they can deliver their grain to the elevator which is constructed at tide water on property owned by the people of Canada. In marketing their grain in that port, they will find that there are no port charges, no tolls and no taxes or levies to be collected, and the port of Prince Rupert is as free as the air you breathe. In regard to the harbour, I say without boasting, Mr. Speaker, that it is the best harbour on the Pacific coast. The whole British fleet could anchor with safety within the shelter of that harbour, and there is no danger of ever having to spend a dollar in dredging or in the upkeep of the harbour. We have an utter absence of fog and an utter absence of ice. You can see from the dock the flash of Triple Island light located fifteen miles out from the port-if a skipper believes he requires the services of a .pilot he can procure one, although many of them do not do so. The pilot can escort him to Triple Island light fifteen miles out from the port, and from that point he sets his course to Japan or for whatever port he may be destined to. Have we done anything with this port? We most assuredly have. At present there is loading in the port of Prince Rupert the tw-elfth steamship to be loaded with lumber for the Orient- They make the journey from Prince Rupert to Yokohama in sixteen days, which is a three-day improvement over any other record made from the Pacific coast. The terminal rates are the same from Prince Rupert to Liverpool as they are from Vancouver to Liverpool. We are 462 miles closer to the Orient than any other port.
I wish to draw the attention .of those interested to the fact that, in the opening up and developing of the port of Prince Rupert, the people are buying goods in their own country, and putting money in their own pockets. I am not making this appeal tonight on behalf of the settlers, who think they are entitled to some reward for their pioneering, although, permit me to say that 35 years of pioneering in the West is deserving of consideration. I am not pleading that special treatment should be given on that account; but from the standpoint of

The Adaress-Mr. Fansher
good sound business logic, and from the standpoint of national economy, I join with all the people who are living in the western land, in the city of Edmonton and in the city of Prince Rupert, in the request that an elevator be constructed forthwith.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In rising to continue this debate, I feel that I must join with those who have preceded me in offering my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address. I have listened with great interest to the many speeches that have been delivered by hon. members of this House since this debate commenced. I listened with deep interest this afternoon to the speech delivered by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler).
I was greatly amused at the controversy over statistics, and the discussion as to who should be held responsible for the emigration from this country. I was reminded of a story I once heard of a darky preacher who, in finishing his sermon, announced that on the next Sabbath he would take as his theme Daniel in the fiery furnace, and one of his congregation immediately arose begged his pardon and asked that he might correct him. He said that Daniel was not in the fiery furnace, but in the lion's den; whereupon the darky preacher said, "My brother has not got the point. The point I intend to make next Sabbath is that it matters not whether Daniel was in the fiery furnace or in the lion's den, he was in a terrible fix anyway." I think the taxpayer of this country is, not so much concerned with who is responsible for the burden of debt that we are labouring under at the present time as he is with the question of how we are going to discharge that debt.
This debate had not gone very far until it became apparent that many things which are mentioned in the Speech from the Throne are not going to receive the attention that one certain item will receive, namely the tariff. As in other debates in former sessions of parliament, a good deal of discussion has centered around taxation and the tariff, and of course the tariff is attacked. I was very much interested in the remarks that were made this' afternoon by the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Marler) in his attempt to defend the protective principle; and I was rather amused that the time of the House should be taken up with a controversy over a policy in which the hon. member and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) both agree. It is strange that whenever this country gets a national headache the leaders of the old political parties seem to know what is
wrong. As we have been aware this last year, they have consulted national political doctors throughout the country, and in their speeches in this House they have indicated what they believe to be a remedy. They have looked at our national tongue, felt our national pulse, tapped our national chest in a number of places and put their ear to our national ribs, and the result of this diagnosis is that there is something wrong with our infant industries. They are agreed thus far; but when it comes to a question of the remedy some say that the tariff dose should be administered in increasing strength while others think that the dose should be diminished. The leader of the opposition declares that what is wrong with Canada to-day is that the tariff has not been administered lately in the same strength as it was administered when he was Prime Minister; and the disturbance in trade he attributes to a change in the quantity and strength of the tariff dose. On the other hand, the Prime Minister declares in the Speech from the Throne that he is persuaded that a reduction in taxation and in production and transportation costs is all that is necessary to effect an economic development hitherto unparalleled. To my mind the significance of the first part of that statement is considerable: the Prime Minister "is persuaded". I want to ask, by whom? I wonder whether it is by the resolutions of Progressive members which have been submitted in this House in the last two years, calling for tariff reduction. And when tariff reduction was not mentioned in the Speech from the Throne I wondered whether the amendment that was moved on one occasion had something to do with that persuasion. Or perhaps it was the electors of Kent and of Halifax who persuaded the Prime Minister. Possibly all these were factors in the persuasion alluded to. It occurred to me this afternoon, when the hon. gentleman from Montreal was speaking, that perhaps some persuasion was necessary indeed if there are many gentlemen on the other side of the House who also believe in the policy he advocated in his speech. But why should there be any persuasion? I have in my hand the tariff proposals as set forth in the Liberal platform of 1919. I shall read them:
That the best interests of Canada demand that substantial reductions of the burdens of Customs taxation be made with a view to the accomplishing of two purposes of the highest importance: First: diminishing the very high cost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; Second: reducing the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion, the vigorous development of which is essential to the progress and prosperity of our country.
That, to these ends, wheat, wheat flour and all products of wheat; the principal articles of food;
The Address-Mr. Fansher

farm implements and machinery; farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery and repair parts thereof; rough and partly dressed lumber; gasoline, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils; nets, net-twines and fishermen's equipments; cement and fertilizers, should be free from Customs duties, as well as the raw material entering into the same.
That a revision downwards of the tariff should be made whereby substantial reductions should be effected in the duties on wearing apparel and footwear, and on other articles of general consumption (other than luxuries), as well as on the raw material entering into the manufacture of the same.
That the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff.
And the Liberal party hereby pledges itself to implement by legislation the provision of this resolution when returned to power.
In the face of all that, I ask, why was persuasion necessary? The Speech from the Throne indicates that we are to expect, when the budget comes down, something in the way of tariff reduction. Now, we do not judge a book by its preface; we judge it by what it contains. Nor do we judge an apple by its appearance; when it is peeled and quartered we know what it is like. I trust that the budget will fulfil the promise given in the Speech from the Throne.
There has been a good deal said1 about emigration from this country and the causes thereof, and perhaps further persuasion may be necessary if we are to be given in the budget the tariff reductions which we are looking for. With that end in view I am going to take the liberty to submit a few more figures which have to deal with the population of the banner province of the Dominion, the province of Ontario. Although the House has listened to a mass of statistics to-day, I trust hon. members will bear with me while I submit a few figures on the shift of population from the rural to the urban districts in old Ontario. I am taking a twenty-year period from 1901 to 1921. The population in Ontario in 1901 was 2,182,947; in 1921, 2,933,662-an increase of 750,715. Let us divide that population into urban and rural. The urban population in 1901 was 935,978; by 1921, twenty years later, it had reached 1,707,370-an increase of 771,392. Now, contrast this with the'rural population during the same period. In 1901 the rural population * stood at 1,246,969, but by 1921 it had dropped to 1,226,292-a decrease of 20,677. The percentages are equally significant. In 1901 we find the urban percentage to be 42.88; the rural, 57.12. By 1921 the figures are practically reversed, the urban standing at 58.19 as against 41-81 for the rural. In other words, during the last twenty years the population in the urban centres has increased nearly
800,000,	while the rural population has de-

creased by over 20,000. These figures are taken from the last census.
But this is not the whole story. We have opened up in the north a new area for settlement, and there has been heavy immigration into it, so that this addition to the rural population there helps to balance the decrease in old Ontario. Taking the older portion of the province by itself, there has been a decrease in the rural population far in excess of the figures I have presented.
I have before me a list of the constituencies in old Ontario, taking the area south of a line from Muskoka to the Ottawa river,, and the decreases Since 1901 are startling. Again my figures cover the twenty-year period from 1901 to 1921. North Bruce shows a decrease of 6,552; South Bruce, 6,183; Dufferin, 5,621; Dundas, 3,962; Durliam, 2,941; East Elgin, 595; Frontenac, 4,356; Grenville, 4,377; North Grey, 2,336; Southeast Grey, 8,203; East Hastings, 4,871; North Huron, 7,426; South Huron, 7,306; East Lambton, 8,639; Lanark, 4,239; Leeds, 3,066; Lennox and Addington, 4,352; West Middlesex, 6,354; Muskoka, 1,552; Norfolk, 2,781; Northumberland, 3,038; North Ontario, 2,970; North Oxford, 1,117; South Oxford, 516; South Perth, 2,233; East Peterborough, 2,575; Prescott, 557; Prince Edward, 1,508; North Simcoe, 3,971; South Simcoe, 1,589; Victoria, 4,516; North Wellington, 6,287 -thirty-two constituencies with decreases running into the thousands during the last twenty years.
What do we find in the urban centres? Toronto has doubled its population every fifteen years since its incorporation, and yet in this old part of Ontario there has been a decrease in rural population. I do not mean to charge this all to our fiscal policy, or the policy which fixes upon the consumers in the rural districts a tariff tax for the benefit of the urban centres, but in large part I do think that this tax is responsible for the unequal development. It is a system whereby money is extracted from the consumers in the rural districts and small towns by the manufacturers for their own benefit, to be expended in our large centres. I submit that these statistics amply bear out my contention. Wheresoever the carcass is, there will the eagles be gathered together. Where there is money to be made, there will you find people go.

speechtext: Vultures.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am very much indebted! to the hon. Minister of Railways for the correction. Perhaps the term is a little

The Address-Mr. Fansher
more significant, too, than eagle. Wheresoever the carcass is, there will the vultures be gathered together. Wheresoever there is money to be made, there will the people gather. That is a natural law; it is the lure of the dollar. We have it borne out in Ontario by these statistics.
I could cite in corroboration figures for the province of Quebec. The rural population in that province, according to the last census, has decreased in the last twenty years, slightly it is true; but on the other hand the urban population has increased to a very considerable extent. To illustrate my point further,
I may say that out of 416 townships in old Ontario-cutting old Ontario off from the Georgian bay to the Ottawa river-375 have lost in population during the last twenty years; they have fewer people to-day than they had in 1901. Only 41 townships show an increase, and most of them are situated close to cities which are overflowing into the surrounding townships. For instance, London has grown out into Westminster township. Windsor and the border cities have grown into the adjoining townships, and Toronto is extending out into the three ridings in York. To my mind these facts are very significant, not only from the agricultural standpoint but from the fact that there are fewer people in those rural districts to support the churches, schools and public institutions, and the costs are increasing. From the standpoint of the nation's welfare these figures are important; a development as unequal as this has been in the last twenty years cannot continue, and I would recommend that our census returns be studied more thoroughly so that they may be used as a guide in the shaping of our fiscal policy.
To add to my argument along this line I have prepared a few figures in connection with four lines of manufacture in this country, to show the amount of assistance which is afforded certain industries in the way of protection. The lines I refer to are automobiles, agricultural implements, boots and shoes, and rubber footwear and rubber goods. These are statistics obtained from information furnished by the Chief Statistician of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics.
There were produced in Canada in 1921, $81,833,226 worth of automobiles. Imports of automobiles into Canada were valued at $11,039,127, and exports at $8,552,883. The duty collected on the amount imported was $3,611,800. These figures show that about $80,000,000 of cars were purchased in Canada. Taking the value of the imports and the duty collected thereon, and applying that ratio to the
cars purchased in Canada, we find that there was a protection afforded the automobile industry, of $23,837,880. That is not taking the tariff percentages at all; it is taking the actual returns.' Now, $11,039,127 worth of imports paid duty to the extent of $3,611,800, so that every time we find that amount of $11,039,127 in the figure indicating the amount produced in Canada we get a further amount equivalent to the protection afforded by the duty.
Following that same line of reasoning in connection with agricultural implements, we find that in 1921 we collected a duty of $889,167 under this head and that there was a protection afforded of $3,824,418. When we come to boots and shoes the figures are a good deal more startling. Boots and shoes produced in Canada totalled $44,665,381. The amount imported was $1,582,697. Very few were exported, namely, $298,470 worth. The duty collected on the amount imported was $436,934, and carrying out the same ratio as with the others we find that a protection was afforded the boot and shoe industry in this country of $11,797,218.
Coming to the last of the lines of manufacture that I have considered, rubber footwear and rubber goods, there were produced in Canada in 1921, $39,469,786 worth; imports were $3,415,044; exports $4,088,205; duty collected, $971,506. The protection afforded was, therefore, $10,006,511. Combining these, we find that the duty collected on the four lines was $5,909,416 and that the protection afforded was $49,466,027. I do not say that that protection was all taken, but that amount of protection is afforded, and if industry argue that they need more tariff, surely they are taking all the protection that is afforded otherwise they would not ask for more.
I think if we would follow all the lines of manufacture through we would find that we are taxed to support the industries of this country to an extent of which we have no idea, and yet we are told by hon. members here to-day that we should protect industry in order that we may have a home market. I sometimes wonder how serious hon. members are when they plead for a home market for the farmers' produce. I have in my hand here an advertisement issued in 1918, in time of stress, by the Finance department and the Victory Loan committee urging the farmers to subscribe to the victory loan. You will remember the argument that was used at that time. It was that we had to sell to Britain and give her credit, and that we must threrefore raise the money at home
The Address-Mr. Fansher

in order to pay the farmer cash so that his produce might go over to Britain, and the farmers themselves were urged to buy victory bonds. This advertisement appeared in one of the leading farm papers of this province, the Farmers' Advocate. The first sentence reads:
The prices of Canadian farm products are fixed in large measure by the demand in Great Britain.
Now with that statement put out by the Finance Minister in the Union government in 1918, we all agree. Note the second sentence :
The price of all is governed by the part exported.
Yet we have hon. members arguing on the floor of this House for the home market in order that the farmer may get more for his crop, when officials who are identified with that very same party say that the price of all is governed by the part exported. "Be ready," it says at the bottom "to buy victory bonds". Down below that in small print appears this:
Issued by the Canadian Victory Loan Committee in co-operation with the Minister of Finance of the Dominion of Canada.

speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member for Brome will know better than I do as he is an older member of the House. I think it was Sir Thomas White. I think the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) became Minister of Finance in August, 1918. These victory bonds were sold in the fall. Perhaps the hon. member for West York was Minister of Finance at that time. But the point I wish to make is this: I believe that many hon. members who argue for the protective principle and a high tariff, and who use the argument of the home market, know and believe that the home market is not nearly so advantageous to the farmers of this country as they would have them believe.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that I have already spoken at too great a length. In conclusion, I am convinced that such unequal distribution between the rural and urban population of this country is not in the best interests of the state. I am convinced that before we shall have the degree of prosperity that we are all looking for in these troublous times some readjustment has got to be made. There is a tendency to place goods beyond the purchasing power of the consumer. The cost of distribution growing out of this centralization is high. These are problems which we will

have to tackle with a will. I trust and believe that in the days to come there will be a natural readjustment brought about. I believe that in the natural course of events deflation will correspond more in all lines of industry, but at the same time I see no reason why industries that have to work two days to buy the products that another industry produces in one should be asked at this time to pay toll to the large centralized industries throughout this Dominion. The Speech from the Throne gives us promise of some redress in this regard, and I hope that that promise, to use the words of the Prime Minister himself, will be abundantly fulfilled.
Mr. J. R. OUIMET (Vaudreuil and Sou-langes), (Translation): Mr. Speaker, on the 3rd of March, 1924, an honourable member who is well known to me gave utterance to the following words, which I find on page 15 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, it is my duty and my privilege to be first to congratulate the mover (Mr. Kelly) and the seconder (Mr. Lapierre) of the Address this afternoon on the acceptable way in which they have performed a none-too-easy task. All of us recall how trying is the ordeal when a new member first addresses this House. Sometimes the ordeal does not become very much mitigated with custom, but nevertheless the first is the most trying, and the success of the hon. members I acknowledge freely and compliment them thereupon. Possibly in respect particularly of the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. Kelly), if X caught aright a portion of his address, I should congratulate the government too.
This language is truly comforting to me, Sir, for it is the first time that I have had the honour to speak in this House.
The right hon. leader of the opposition showed so much sympathy towards new members that I shall take the liberty of adding a few remarks and of expressing my views relatively to what has been said, this session, in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
I do not think the House will deny me that privilege and that the courteous members who honour me by listening, at present will not reproach me for having abused of their precious hours of deliberation during the last two sessions, as I have been very patient and I hope to be likewise treated.
I listened with much attention to the different phases of the debate. I pondered over them. I found some of them quite to the point; others I found wanting. However, before taking up the subject I must-and I believe it my duty to do so-extend my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.

The Address-Mr. Onimet
I should further add, Mr. Speaker, that for the first time in my parliamentary career the occasion lends itself to publicly convey to you my respects and congratulations for the mark of confidence that parliament has bestowed upon you by raising you to that eminent post of Speaker of the House of Commons. I would fear to wound your proverbial modesty for congratulations have poured in upon you from all sides, as much from the loyal as from the disloyal opposition of His Majesty as those that come from the party to which I have the honour to belong, they are so sincere that I shall not further dwell upon them; but I have private reasons to recall them to my memory, and especially the congratulations of those who were witness of your start in life, the troubled period of your political career and the period so calm and full of consolation of your university life.
I had the signal honour-it is now nearly twenty-four years ago-to be one of your most diligent students, and although not one of your most brilliant, yet one of the most deserving, owing to nature having deprived me of many gifts.
You will remember, Sir, your lectures on the history of Law, at Laval University, now Montreal University. I must admit that, never perhaps during our university life, my contemporaries and myself benefited so much by the excellent maxims of probity, honour and patriotism that you forcibly impressed upon us at the time.
We are all growing old, and it now gives me much pleasure to recall these reminiscences this evening. As it was so well said by a great French writer

I think it was Charles Nodier, in his Souvenirs de Jeunesse-it is one of the most delightful prerogatives of old age to recall with great accuracy reminiscences of one's youth.
You will pardon me, Mr. Speaker,-both you, and the late Mr. Monk, were so kind to your students of Laval in those days,-if I recall publicly these recollections which linger forever in the memory of those who are of fair lineage. As it was so nicely expressed by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre): Tutored at the school of the great deceased, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who, although a Liberal, had a considerable number of political admirers holding opposite views to his, but who rendered him justice; you have sown the seeds of probity and honour in our midst, and we have endeavoured to follow your advice and teachings.
It is therefore in this frame of mind which you have so well fashioned that we feel happy
to acknowledge publicly this homage, we, all your old students of Laval, who, since you occupy a seat in this House, number, I believe, over fifty, either as member, minister or Speaker. I beg for the leniency of the House as a new member and a novice in my political career. Representing one of the finest, if not the finest county of the province of Quebec, situated at a distance of 70 miles from Ottawa and 50 miles from Montreal, the county of Vaudreuil and Soulanges which did me the honour of returning me by acclamation March 22, 1922.
Why did this election take place at such an early date? How does it happen that our good friends, our opponents, did not think it worth while, neither in my case nor that of my good and excellent neighbour, the member for Jacques-Cartier (Mr. Rheaume) to contest our respective counties? There must have existed a cause to all this, and I discover it in the fact that the Conservative party was still sleeping, and that it has since awakened after an alarming slumber, which might have been taken for a serious enough coma so far as the province of Quebec is concerned. It was so fast asleep that, on the 1st of September, 1923, this same party, semi-conscious, thought it was time to awake, and, Sir, I will establish the fact that it awoke in the county of my good friend from Jacques-Cartier (Mr. Rheaume), at Car-tierville. I have before me certain invitations which had been sent to me by our good friends the Conservatives who thought that something might be gained in the county of Vaudreuil and Soulanges and that we, the Liberals should endeavour to allow ourselves to be swayed by the honourable leader of the opposition.
Therefore, on Saturday, Sept, 1, 1923, reappeared again, at Cartierville, the Conservative political picnics of the province of Quebec, and this notice, which I shall read in a minute, had been scattered everywhere in the county of Vaudreuil and Soulanges, from Point Fortune as far as Point Cascades where we have a great number of Conservatives and Liberals. Here follows the programme which had been sent to our good friends:
At Cartierville Revival of* the Conservative Political Picnics In the Province of Quebec You are cordially invited
On Saturday, September 1, 1923, will take place, at Belmont Park, Cartierville, a large Conservative political picnic.
Belmont Park is an ideal spot for a day of rest and recreation; situated close to the tramway terminus at Cartierville, on the banks of the river des Prairies, east of Lachapelle bridge, it offers numerous amusements: merry-go-round, ferris-wheel, orchestra, band, beautiful lawns, century old trees, shaded groves. All,

girls, boys, men, women and children are cordially invited to this country festival which will be a grand prelude to Labour-day.
The political picnic will begin at 9 a.m. (Standard time) and end at 9 p.m. (Standard time).
The only expense you will have to incur will be in the making up of your basket for lunch and supper.
Be one of this great popular manifestation.
Both in the morning and afternoon, games will be held, amusements of all kinds, races opened to all ages, and various tournaments which will be rewarded by the distribution of costly prizes to the winner at the end of each event.
The programme of the games will be published in the sport page of our daily newspapers, on Friday, August 31, and will also be distributed at the door of Belmont Park, on the day of the picnic.

Andre Fauteux, the President of the Cartier-Macdonald club and the President of the Conservative Association, English section.

of the Conscription Act, but its most narrow-minded interpreter and its most odious perpetrator. I

laws on conscription, censure and prescription would have borne more heavily on the people. This is very wicked, I would never have uttered these words in the House.
The people of Quebec have also the right and the duty to reject Mr. Meighen's economic policy, halfprotectionist, half-socialist, his clumsy electoral empiricism which aims at winning over both the views of the West and the gold of the eastern manufacturers. Mr. Meighen, like the quack doctor of Moliere has "reversed everything". What Cartier, Macdonald, Tupper and the whole Conservative party as well as the whole Liberal party, from 1860 to 1899, held as unjust, condemnable, disastrous for Canada, even contrary to the true interests of the Empire, he considers desirable, expedient, necessary; it is even, he says, the only "honourable position" that Canada can occupy in the Empire. Nonsense 1 At the very most be hardly finds means to screen his banners behind a torn flap of their trousers!
Obstinately resolved to continue his journey, full of jolts, in his top boots where his head is lost, as well as his feet, the Tom-Thumb of the neo-conservatism attempted, at St. Hyacinthe and Drummondville, to justify his wild prank of last year, when he insisted at all costs, that Canada should hurry to the rescue, arms in hand, at the sound of the first trumpet blast of Lloyd George, after the failure of Smyrna.

To want to hold us tied down for ever to a senseless, impracticable pact, disowned by all its authors, and never internationally ratified, that alone is enough to show the dangerous blindness of the personage. Can one imagine where could drag us this puny advocate, anxious for his pound of flesh, if the public aberration placed in his hands power and authority?

Their struggle both touching and ludicrous reminds us of the doings and gesture of certain personages matched together, in the comic reviews: Plic and Ploc, Mutt and Jeff, the Big and the Little one.
Of the two, it is still the little one who is the weaker. At Victoriaville, Mr. Fauteux reminded us of the preliminary work undertaken and the responsibility resting upon Laurier and the Liberals in the imperialist revolution which dragged us into the whirlpool of war and conscription. The remark fitted in well, and the tactic was fair. But what seems to be less in evidence, is that Mr. Fauteux and Mr. Monty, who, in the past, denounced Laurier's camouflaged

Mr. Monty thinks that the French Canadians should place their confidence in Mr. Meighen, because he speaks from day to day better French, and that tomorrow like yesterday, he is willing to place in office many "Canayens". That is what becomes, in the hands of narrow-minded politicians nationalism in matters of language and patronage. That Meighen speaks the French language like Bossuet or Mederic, like Berryer or like the most dense ear-drum breakers of our courts and hustings, this in no way alters the worth of his views, his policy and of his person. Bismark spoke French perfectly; this in no way proved that he was France's best friend. Besides, one cannot too much insist upon the fact: it is not because he is an enemy of the French Canadians that Mr. Meighen does not deserve the public confidence: it is as an enemy of Canada, as destroyer of Canadian nationality and also of the best Conservative traditions: it is because, everything tends to show it, he is ready to shatter the economic equilibrium of the country, its social peace, its international position; it is because we know that he is quite willing, to satisfy his incoherent passions of half educated theorist, to drag Canada in the worst internal as well as external ventures.
Deluded politicians may find him an able dialectician; people without any foregone conclusion but endowed with some power of observation look upon him as a dangerous demagogue. The small Plies and the big Plocs of the reborn and soulless Conservative party- will strive in vain: the people as a whole, left to their good common sense, will not have him.
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to quote any further from this article for I notice the hour is quite late. However, it does seem that the Conservative party awoke, but somewhat late for our by-elections in the counties of Jacques Cartier, Vaudreuil and Soulanges and others. They are to awake, one hears, in the province of Quebec. According to what I have just mentioned a few minutes ago and the extracts quoted, it would seem that the province of Quebec will tremble in the presence of my right hon. friend, the leader of the disloyal opposition of His Majesty!
What will be this awakening of the Conservative party? What will the awakening of the whole population be, not only of the province of Quebec, but from one end of the country to the other, from Victoria to Halifax? On what grounds will the electorate stand to judge of the awakening of the disloyal opposition of His Majesty? Will it be on the good faith of the leader of the Conservative party? Will it be on the good faith of the leader of the Progressive party or will it rather be on the good faith of the leader of the Liberal party, the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada? I notice on the faces of those who are listening that the answer is a foregone conclusion. It will be on the good faith of the leader of the Liberal party who, at present, presides over the destinies of Canada. The people will acknowledge the good faith of the upright and honourable man who

is in charge of our affairs, and the country will judge him upon this good faith. In their hearts the masses are just. Rouse their passions and they may get beyond control.
During the last session it could have been an easy matter to defeat the government. We had but, if I am not mistaken, eight of majority on the budget vote. That budget, as it was brought down in the House, made for economy, economy on all sides, economy showing thrift, etc., however, there were many others to practice; I will but mention one: that of speech. Indeed, what everyone thinks but does not express, I think it is my duty to mention, for I am free to express my thoughts. We had, in the course of the last session, on the budget as well as on other subjects many a sermon and advice. About eighty speeches were delivered on horse racing-" Malum per accidens and non malum per se " as would put it the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon)-as a guide to our views on tjie question of labour, on the "loafing on the job," on immigration, on Imperial matters, on the French Treaty, on halibut fishing, which the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) will now have to take up, with the help of the good advices of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). Incidentally I congratulate them and also the government for these appointments. They are of all, the two best appointments that could be made by a government conscious of its responsibilities and of the worth of the men it placed in these high offices.
We also had during last session, interesting discussions on decreasing the parliamentary indemnity, and if the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) was in his seat, this evening, I should sincerely congratulate him for the gallant way in which he opposed this measure. It is particularly on this last debate that we were treated to an amusing lecture of an altogether maiden-like and innocent simplicity on the part of these sanctimonious people, always fretting for others, while quite at ease for themselves, and who imagine that through shamming all sins will be forgiven.
If we had, in this House, only promoters- or lady promoters-of the parliamentary indemnity reduction, we would have to submit to a bankruptcy act for cradles. Fortunately, as the hon. member for Jacques Cartier so well expressed it, the cradle bankruptcy is not to be feared in the province of Quebec "for husband and wife religiously live up to their matrimonial obligations." May I ask the members of this House if things would so

happen in certain counties of Ontario, should the electors deem it proper to choose as their representatives persons of canonic age? But the "demon du midi" is there watching and I would not be astonished to see the county of Southeast Grey become vacant one of these days, and, there, we shall witness a great fight between the parties.
I paused, listened and kept my eyes open during the last sessions which I attended. And as I have the advantage-I think I may say so without appearing to boast-to speak both languages in use in this country, of which one is understood by all and the other -the most important and the one most used in diplomatic circles-is spoken and understood only by a selected minority, I was deeply and sadly deceived after listening attentively to the leader of the disloyal opposition of His Majesty. As to the leader of the loyal opposition of His Majesty-an opposition, forsooth, but more sedate and conforming more with the sound teachings of the instinct of self-preservation, and the satisfaction of duty accomplished for the welfare of the country and not of his party-I cannot but congratulate him on the position taken.
I have always had for the official leader of the disloyal opposition of His Majesty a profound admiration, and in this I think I share the opinion of the hon. member for Drummond and Arthabaska (Mr. Lafiamme) who made no secret of his admiration for the leader of the opposition, but who, in a speech he made, and which expresses - well our opinion, could not approve his way of reasoning, neither his insight nor his judgment. I will quote his words, which are to be found at page 2896 of Hansard, Vol. Ill, Session of 1922.
The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) who has, in this House, no greater admirer than myself and who commands a prestige far in advance of what his age would entitle him to-I say it openly; I stated it in private, I may do so in public-and who is a powerful debater almost without any rival in this House-merely told us in picturesque language which I shall condense into a simile after the Latin mind, by saying: that the hon. Minister of Finance's head was as white as wdnter. He forgot to add this: that time had not impaired his vigour, which recalls a spring day.
And further on, at page 2896, during the debate on the budget, when it was a question of whether the Liberal party would remain in power and what would be the stand taken by the hon. western members on the budget, he said:
In other words the gentleman sitting opposite to us stated: Your policy is a poor one, but you are wrong in not having followed it. On the contrary, they add,

the principles we have been preaching for the last half century are the only true ones; by applying them, you are wrong. This is, Mr. Speaker, one of the things that I have not yet understood, during my short experience in this House. I hope that public life will impart sufficient suppleness of mind to enable me to understand that this distinguished political leader and statesman was right when one day he endeavoured to reassure me in these words: My friend, logic and politics in Canada are two grand ladies who have never met in the same drawing room	
I think the time has come for one who, to-day, enters public life to shoulder his responsibilities, but I must, casually, remind the very able and estimable leader of the Agrarian party (Mr. Crerar) that tonight or in the wee hours of morn he will meet at the cross roads that lady of which I spoke a few seconds ago, and by name-cold logic.
And the hon. member for Drummond and Arthabaska ended his speech by these words which have always remained in my memory, because I esteem him highly; he is, indeed, an eminent lawyer, highly endowed, and who has much sway over the Liberal party and wields much influence in his profession, because his judgment is always sound:
I submit, Sir, that these three reasons are not worth much. I am sorry to say so-because the right hon. leader of the opposition, who does me the courtesy of listening just now, will not find in this House a greater admirer than me-I find with regret that the exigencies of politics have induced him, in his anxiety to defeat the main motion which is before Parliament, to take a stand giving the impression that there comes a time when the image of his country is dimmed by the clash of party interests, to the point of preventing him from taking a broader and more lofty view of the question.
We admit that the leader of the opposition has good qualities which he might have devoted to a better cause.	I would not go so
far as to say that I admire him more than the hon. member for Drummond and Arthabaska; it would be wronging our leader that I respect and honour, and who was able to surround himself with efficient ministers. I, therefore, admire the leader of the opposition, but, like the hon. member for Drummond and Arthabaska, I cannot admire his reasoning powers, his insight or agree with his conclusions; and in this I think I am expressing the opinion of one of my good friends, who at times, but at times only, evinces a kindly disposition toward the opposition leader. I refer to the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff). The right hon. leader of the disloyal opposition of His Majesty is, as the Minister of Defence so well expressed it one day, like the Bourbons of the old regime: He has neither learned nor forgotten anything. He has not even forgotten his own defeat, or his enthusiasm for the glory of the Empire. And if you will allow me, I shall remind you by the way of his momentous words uttered during the war: 9J
"To the last man, to the last dollar for the glory of the Empire." All the votes of these poor soldiers that are fighting in the trenches for the glory of the Empire, we must have, to carry a county by the name of Nipissing, or Chambly and Vercheres. We must, with that end in view, send code telegrams; we must hold on to power, notwithstanding the solemn promises we gave that we were only a war government. But, nonsense, we hold the power, and we shall keep it. "What we have we hold" always for the glory of the Empire.
We know the result produced by this statement, in the province of Quebec. Destiny, chance, unfortunate words and many other contingencies that I shall not undertake to discuss have made the right hon. leader of the opposition, an extraordinary personage under cover of meekness and modesty. He has a particular way of his own to pulverise his opponents and hurl the thunderbolt of eloquence. He gave us to understand, on many occasions in this House, that the party to which we belonged had broken its pledges, that the people had made a mistake on December 0, 1921. I delight in recalling his indignation, either dissimulated or real,-because I am told he is a great comedian,-when an hon. member hailing from the county of Springfield (Mr. Hoey) reminded him of his broken pledges. This did not prevent this hon. member to vote with the leader of the opposition on the budget however the hon. member voted according to the dictate of his conscience. The right hon. leader of the opposition has also proclaimed his great, immense, unfathomable love for the province of Quebec. Well, I have a word to add in regard to this great love expressed in words so odd that it could not be thought sincere by people in earnest as those of the province to which I belong. When, Sir, he made those statements in the province of Quebec, he must have twisted his features in ludicrous fashion; it would have been worth as much as to see a dog swallow wasps. What has been this tardy admiration, and this sudden manifestation for the good old province of Quebec? You will allow me, Sir, to express it in two words. This love was declared, as I said a few minutes ago, at the time of the Cartierville picnics and the awakening of the Conservative party, but it had previously shown itself. It had seen daylight on a memorable date, a few days I think, before the general elections of December 6, 1921. About that time, there must have been a caucus of my right hon. friend's party; at

that caucus they must have discussed the very uncertain chances of the Conservative party in Quebec; note, Sir, that I was not present at the caucus, but although I was not there, the following scene must have taken place, which I will enact for the amusement of the House,-it may perhaps divert the member for Grenville (Mr. Meighen): The Chairman of the liberal-tory-conservative-national-national-ist caucus must have told his partisans, by putting the question: "General elections are to take place, the date has been fixed for December 6, 1921. Our advice is, answers the choir of leaders of the unionist group, that we must have general elections on December 6, 1921". Second question put by the Chairman of the caucus: "How shall we organize?" Unanimous answer: "The best way possible so as to remain in power which is so dear to us." There were delegates from all provinces at the caucus, even perhaps from Quebec. Third question by the chairman of the caucus: "How shall we act to meet the views of all the provinces-the Maritime provinces, the eastern and western provinces?" "For heaven's sake, give them cabinet appointments, " answers the chorus of wise Areopagities. "Ministers, ministers, inquire some delegates of the province of Quebec, but we have not had any in your cabinet since you have been in power." " We shall make some," answers solemnly the present right hon. leader of the opposition. "How will this take place?" questions the chorus of caucus members. The province remembered that this sudden effusion must have been brought on by interest which is the measure of the Conservative party's acts, We had the great satisfaction of seeing the Hon. Mr. Belley crushingly defeated by the hon. member for Charlevoix and Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain), we saw the hon. President of the Privy Council beaten hollow by the present hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau); we saw the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Papineau) elected against the Hon. Mr. Monty; we had the full satisfaction to see the hon. Solicitor General, rMr. Ouimet.]
who had been so strongly urged upon to accept the nomination utterly defeated by the present hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Prevost). That is the result of the policy followed by my right hon. friend; and today it is asserted that the Liberal party- fears election. I shall quote the words of the right hon. member (Mr. Meighen) who spoke before me and immediately after my hon. friend from Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre) and proclaimed in his peroration, that the Liberal party dreads elections:
I venture to assert that the opinion of the people of Canada, already so often expressed, now so evident that he who runs may read, now so apparent that conceivably the government is urging its supporters to keep in the best of health and the pink of condition, for they want no more by-elections-I venture to assert that the judgment of the people of Canada is already written and waits only to be handed down and that the electors only abide the day when the conduct which I have described will be once and for all put an end to-the conduct legislative, the conduct administrative and the conduct electoral.
I wish to apologize, Mr. Speaker, for having spoken so much at length. We have followed Sir Wilfrid Laurier's policy since 1921, we, the Liberals represent, in this House, all the counties of the province of Quebec, and, I believe, we could again appeal with confidence to the impartial vote of the people. We have tried by all possible means to re-establish peace and harmony between the different groups and the various views which exist in this country. We are pushing forward and we will co-operate with all men of good will to bring back prosperity as it existed in our country previous to the troubled days of war. We do not wish to cast any slur upon the right hon. leader of the opposition who violently attacked us during the course of the last two sessions and who, to-day, again exhibited his fighting spirit reminding us of Captain Fracasse. He thinks that fear is in our hearts. We invite him to come to the province of Quebec as much as he pleases; he will always be a welcome guest; but as our late leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, at times said:	"When I visit Toronto, I am always
a welcome guest, but Toronto always votes against me."
As for our good friends the Progressives, we invite them to join us, for we have always been without fear or reproach, as becomes worthy knights.
